summary: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 67 and 1966 67. In respect of the assessment year 1967 67, the Wealth Tax Officer determined the net wealth of the assessee at Rs. 1, 50, 000 / on the valuation date. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assets were not subjected to wealth - tax as they had been acquired by the assessee during the previous year but since the asset was in the possession of the asses see, he could not be included in the net Wealth of the deceased. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Wealth tax officer. The High Court affirmed the view taken by the Tribunal. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle underlying section 7 (1) is that the value of the right in the property which constitutes the asset of an assessee under the Income Tax Act shall be the aggregate value of all the assets belonging to the assessee including cash, debt, and other property inherited or arising from the same kind of asset, if any, held by him immediately before the relevant valuation date, and where the asset so acquired has been acquired prior to the relevant date, it would be the last day of the previous years'corresponding ly preceding the relevant period which would include the last date of the relevant year. [ 11 B E ] 2. The expression " net wealth " occurring in sub section (I) of Section 7 means the total amount of the net assets of the person liable to pay wealth tax on the relevant annual value of his net wealth. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the net income of the assesses. Therefore, the value calculated on the basis of the actual cost of the asset will have to be determined as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the wealth tax authorities, is the correct value of such property. [ 12 C D ] 3. The question whether the asset is an asset other than cash or hybrid, arises only when the asset becomes a part of the value thereof. If the asset itself becomes part of a particular asset, then the value should be determined based upon the value, which is the value per share of the property owned by the asses ee. [ 13 A B ] 4. The value of a property is determined pursuant to sub section 1 of section 7 read with section 5 of the Act. Where the asset belongs to an assessee, bar those expressly exce pted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employ's one system of accounting or another. [ 14 G H;

The respondent was a Government servant. He was dismissed from service by an order dated 22. 6. 1969 on the ground that he had not been served with a charge sheet and that he did not have the opportunity to defend himself against the charges framed against him. On appeal, the Appellate Authority set aside the order of dismissal and directed reinstatement in service with full back wages. In the writ petition filed by the respondent before the High Court challenging the order passed by the Tribunal, it was contended that the Tribunal had committed an error in holding that the respondent had failed to serve notice on the appellant and that the impugned order was bad in law as no reasonable opportunity had been given to the respondent to defend his case. It was also urged that the enquiry conducted by the Inquiry Officer was vitiated because the respondent's name was not found in the list of selected candidates prepared for appointment to the post of Labour Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the Enquiry Officer had not followed the principles of natural justice inasmuch as he had no jur isd ic tion to hold a regular inquiry into the allegations made against the respondent. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly quashed the order directing the disciplinary authority to reconsider the matter and to pass appropriate orders in accordance with law. [ 37 A ] 2. The respondent had been working in the Department of Civil Engineering and he was a very senior officer. He had worked in the department of the State Government. He could not be said to be a person who had been appointed to the department. There is nothing on record to show that any departmental inquiry was ever initiated against the delinquent official. The only thing which can be done is that the departmental inquiry should be dispensed with in terms of the provisions of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution. [ 38 C D ] 3. The fact that the Respondent had been charged with misconduct and tried to mislead the Tribunal cannot be a ground for quashing the order. [ 39 E F ] 4. The order of the Tribunal setting aside the penalty imposed upon the respondent is set aside.

The appellant, a tenant of the land in question, filed an application under section 10 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for recovery of possession of the suit property on the ground that he was a trespasser and had been illegally dispossessed by the respondent. The Trial Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to seek possession of his land as he was not a tenant within the meaning of Section 2 (b) of Act. On appeal, the District Judge held that the suit was barred by virtue of section 7 (1)( d) of C. P. C. and decreed the suit. In second appeal, it was contended before this Court that since the suit itself was barred, the High Court should have remanded the matter to the Trial Court for fresh disposal after giving opportunity to the parties to lead evidence. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 The provisions of Order 7 Rule 10 CPC are mandatory in nature and if such a provision is not made, the remedy provided therein is available to the plaintiff. [ 11 D E ] 1. 2 It is well settled that where a person is a tenant under the statute, the landlord has to be dealt with by the law enacted by the legislature. If the landlord is a trespasser, the law will have to be applied. But where the landlord seeks relief against the dispossession of a tenant, the court must consider whether the landlord can ask for restoration of possession or grant injunction. [ 12 G H; 12A B ] 2. 3 The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is very limited. It cannot act as a Court of Appeal but only when there is a specific provision in the Statute which gives power to the Tribunal to decide the dispute between the landlord and the tenant. [ 12A F ] 4. The expression'other than a tenant'used in sub section (2)( a) of section 8 of the Act does not mean that the Civil Courts have no jurisdiction to deal with any matter arising from the said provision. [ 13 A B ] 5. The word " tenant " occurring in section 7 of the Orissa General Clauses Act, 1950 means a person who holds land under another person and is deemed to be a tenant. Therefore, the bar created by section 7 is applicable to the present case. [ 14 B ] 6. 1. The words " any person " appearing in section 8 (2), namely, a person claiming to be the tenant under a document executed by him would include a person whose name appears in the voters list. [ 15 B C ] 2.( i) The expression " tenant ", as defined in section 2 (h) of Bihar Tenancy Act, 1908 includes a person holding land under a lease or licence granted by the State Government or the Central Government. [ 15A B ] (ii) The definition of " tenant'in section 3 (g) of The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1960 is wide enough to cover all persons who are deemed tenants under the Act.

The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the. The petitioner is an employee of the Corporation and was working as a " car p enters in Government service ". He was appointed on daily wages to work as " car penter " in the same establishment. On his request, he was paid at the rate of Rs. 600 per month. In the year 1986, the petitioner was given a contract for doing the work of " car ping of all kinds of labour's " including pain ting etc., and also for other works. The petitioners were paid at par with their counter parts in other establishments. The respondent Corporation issued a circular dated June 29, 1986 directing that the petitioners should be paid minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner, Himachal Pradesh, Shimla. The said circular provided that the daily wage workers would be paid at rates applicable to similar work in other areas. The respondents challenged the validity of the circular dated March 30, 1986 before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh. A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the circular did not off end Article 14 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal. Allow ing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The circular letter dated July 11, 1986 cannot be enforced. [ 670 E ] 2. The Circular dated November 6, 1986 does not prohibit payment of minimum wages payable to the work done by the workmen in the Corporation. It only provides that the pay will be fixed at the lowest stage in the work concerned. The word'equal pay'has been used in the context of the work performed by the workman. The expression'equal work'means that there shall be no discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same management. If it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst such different sets of employees, the principle of " equal pay for equal work " cannot be applied. [ 671 C D ] 3. The decision of the Division Bench of the Punjab & Haryana High Court in M / s. All India Institute of Medical Sciences vs A. I. M. S.,; at 245. relied upon by the learned counsel for the petitioner is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [ 673 F G ] 4. The fact that the petitioner had worked for nearly 17 years is not disputed. There is no dispute that the work was similar to the job which was being done by another person. The question whether the petitioner can claim parity with the counter parts of the other establishments in the State or not is a matter which must be determined by expert bodies like the Commission. [ 672 B C ] 5. The principle of equal pay fo r equality before law does not require any interference.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 read with section 120B I. P. C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed an appeal before the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed his appeal, confirming the conviction of accused 6 but reduced the sentence from death to imprisonment of life. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. In a case where several mur ders are committed in furtherance of common intention of all the accused persons, it is not necessary that each one must be separately charged for every offence unless some overt act is attributed to him which may indicate that he had done more than one act. [ 288 B ] 2. It is well settled that the charge of conspiracy under section 120 A I. C., is not illegal merely because there is no direct evidence regarding the participation of the other accused in the commission of the crime. [ 289 D E ] 3. The prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the murder of Mal an was committed by the appellant alone who was responsible for causing injuries on the deceased. The circumstantial evidence relied upon by the prosecution is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused. [ 290 G H; 291 A ] 4. The circumstances established by the evidence do not conclusively point to the guilt or innocence of the appellant. The fact that the appro ver was a co conspir ator does not necessarily lead to the inference that he was a party to the conspiracy. [ 293 F ] 5. The confession of the co accused cannot be accepted as true even if it is assumed that the same was voluntary and truthful.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the late Maharaja of Vizianagaram, was the holder of certain properties in her possession. She executed two documents Exs. P. 1 and P. 2 dated February 16, 19 24 and Ex. P - 3 dated August 31, 19 01. In respect of these two properties she executed a will on January 14, 1923, beque ath ing all the properties to her son, the respondent No. 1. On the death of the testator, the said properties devol ved upon his wife as well as on the appellant who is the next heir of the deceased. After the death, the appellant filed a suit for declaration that the will executed by her husband was not binding on him and that he had no right or interest therein. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondents against the decree of the trial court. The High Court held that the document was not proved and that it was inadmissible in evidence because the signature of the test at rix on the will did not tally with the admitted writing by the test At ting al Judge. It further held that even if there were suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the will, the prop ounder's case would be good enough to hold that the Will was genuine and that the prop oun ders had full knowledge of its contents. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The High Courts have rightly found that the appellant has failed to prove the due and proper execution of his will. The presumption under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 can only be raised when the attesting witnesses are examined in proof of the execution and attestation of the document. (ii) The onus of proving the will rests on the party pro pound ing the will by examining the attesting witness and also by examining other witnesses. (iii) The burden of proof is on the prop er ant who seeks to dis pel the suspicious circumstances attending the execution. The prop ounder must remove all the doubts and make necessary averments in the will which go to the root of the matter and so do the prop he cy. (iv) The prop oun der should be absolutely innocent and the prop ag ation must appear to be voluntary and true. (v) The condition precedent to the validity of the disposition is that the testator himself must either attest the will or attest it in order to satisfy the judicial conscience. If the prop prop ounder fails to remove the suspicious circumstance the court has to accept the will as a valid piece of evidence. In the present case the prop. tiff failed to discharge the onus cast on him by the prop het and the High court was therefore justified in rejecting the prop ped ed will.

The appellants are manufacturers of electric energy apparatus and electrical appliances. They were assessed to duty under item No. 4 in the Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The assessment was made on the basis that the goods manufactured by them were covered by entry No. 6 of Part B of Schedule I to the Act. The Assistant Collector held that the'elect ro ly tic'items were not covered by the relevant entry but they were covered only by entry Nos. 3 and 4 of Part A of Schedule 1 to the said Act. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that these items were covered within the expression " electrical apparatus " as defined in section 2 (a) of the Act and therefore fell outside the scope of Entry No. 5 of Schedule II to the Madras General Sales tax Act, 1959. In appeal before this Court it was contended for the appellant that the expression'electrical apparatus'used in entry No, 4 means electrical apparatus designed or adap ted for use as an aid or addition; that since the word'elect rode'is not defined in the Act, the term'elect ri fied apparatus'must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in a narrow technical sense. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression'elect ric ist'has been defined in Section 2 (d) of Andhra Pradesh Act, 1951 which defines'elect an apparatus '. It does not mean any instrument capable of being used for any purpose other than that specified in the schedule. [ 10 56 F ] 2. The word'apparatus'in the definition clause includes apparatus, apparatus, tools, etc., used for the purpose of the apparatus. The words'elect r ors'and'elect rol apparatus'have been defined to mean apparatus, instruments, apparatus and mechanical appliances and apparatus employed for the performance of some particular kind of work. These words do not necessarily exclude apparatus like apparatus or apparatus used for regulating the supply of electricity or water. The meaning given to the word " elect ro mag ne tic apparatus " in the dictionary is that it means apparatus designed to serve as an ap pliance or apparatus for controlling the t one and transmit ting equipment. The same thing is used in connection with the apparatus meant for the use of the person who uses it. There is no reason why the word access ory should be construed to include apparatus designed for the purposes of the entry.

The petitioners in the present case were carrying on quarrying operations for mining minerals. They had applied to the State Government under section 15 of the Act for grant of a quarry lease for minor minerals. The State Government rejected their applications and issued permits to them. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said orders by filing writ petitions before this Court. It was contended that the provisions of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 were ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as they violated Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismis sing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the State is not an un guided or arbitrary one. It is not a matter of policy but merely a policy. It has to be left to the executive. There is no inherent right in a citizen to carry on business with his property. [ 416 C ] 2. The object of the legislation is to regulate the development of minerals and to prevent exploitation thereof. The legislature has the power to make rules regulating the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect of minor minerals and the regulation of mines and mineral development. The rule making authority has been vested with wide powers to make such rules. The rules have to be made only for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the act. The fact that the rules are framed for the first time does not mean that the State has no power to frame rules for regulating the conditions of the licence. [ 418 E F ] 3. The contention that the power under section 15A (b) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 cannot be exercised without the prior approval of the Central Government is also devoid of merit. The legislative competence of the State Legislature to make the impugned rules is not questioned. The Parliament has the legislative competence to enact the law. [ 419 D E ] 4. The Act is valid since it has the effect of imposing a tax on the royalty which is payable at the rate prescribed by the Act. [ 420 B ] 5. The petitioner's challenge to the levy of royalty being violative of article 301 of the constitution must fail.

The appellant was appointed as a trustee of the temple in 1920. He died on March 31, 1968 and his widow executed a will beque ath ing her properties to him. In 1932 he filed a suit for declaration that the trust deed was void and inoperative and not binding on him. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. On appeal by certificate, it was contended before this Court: (1) that the trustees were entitled to succeed to the property under section 6 (9) of the Act; (2) that there was no succession to the office of trustee in the present case because the trustees had only an estate in the property which could be inherited from the f ounder himself; (3) that even if the trustees hip of the deceased was hereditary one, the trustees would have a right to manage the property and perform its pu ja or worship; (4) that since the ded ication was made for a fixed period of one year and not for life, the trust was governed by the provisions of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951; (5) that though the trustees are entitled to manage their affairs in the matter of management, they cannot claim any share in the income of the trust property unless the trustees appoint a manager or a manager for a particular purpose; (6) that in view of the decision of this Court in Sri Mahant Param eswar Das vs Shri O udh Das, A. I. R. 1954 S. C. 11 19, the managing committee is a'person'within the meaning of section 6 of the, and therefore, the appointment of the trustees must be held to be valid. Held, that the expression " hereditary trustee " occurring in section 6, sub section (9), of the Bihar and Orissa Public Trusts Act, 1950, means a personal hereditary trustee who has a beneficial interest in the trust estate. The word'hereditary'used in section 6A (9)( i) does not include hereditary trustee.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) there was no evidence to connect him with the murder; (2) that the prosecution witnesses were interested in falsely implicating the accused and (3) that PW 4 had been won over by the deceased who was sleeping at a distance of about one mile from the place where he fell down. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The testimony of PW 4 is not corroborated by the contents of the FIR. It is difficult to accept that PW 1, 2 and 3 are wholly reliable witnesses. If they were so closely related to the deceased they would have mentioned the names of all the assailants as well as the name of the assailant. But if the witness was wholly reliable, his presence at the time of occurrence cannot be doubted. [ 712 G H ] (ii) The High Court has rightly rejected the testimony of the sole eye witness because the witness turned hostile. He did not see the assailants who might have escaped. When the accused was tried for the offence, the court should be circumspe ct and closely scrutin ise the evidence to come to an un hes it ating conclusion whether the testimony given by him is true or false. [ 713 B C ] (iii) The conduct of the accused in trying to escape from custody does not appear to be unnatural. He must be anxious to avoid the charge being discarded merely because he happened to be sleeping near the door of the house when he went to sleep. [ 714 D E ] (iv) There is nothing in the statement of PW 2 which shows that he was either alone or in a position to identify the assailants. Even if the testimony is believed, the identification of the assailants is not only proper but also trustworthy. [ 715 A B ] (v) The fact that the deceased was sleeping along with others at the place of occurrence is very significant. [ 716 F ] (vi) The incident took place at about 10 p. m. and the deceased died immediately after the incident. The dead body was found next day morning at about 11 a. m., and the inquest report prepared by the Sub Inspector showed that the dead body of the deceased could not be recovered till the next day. [ 717 G ] (vii) The delay in sending the dead bodies to the police station for postmortem examination was not fatal to the case of the prosecution.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family and carried on the business of growing and manufacturing cotton yarn. In the assessment year 1950 51, the appellant claimed to be an assessee under section 24 B (1) of the Income tax Act, 1922 for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1951 52 in respect of the income received by him during the previous year ending on 31 2 1949. The Income Tax Officer held that the amount which was received by the heirs and legal representatives as compensation for the loss of their estate was not liable to tax under section 34 (1)( b) read with section 24 (c) of Income tax, Act, 1961. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Taxation Officer but reduced the amount of Rs. 37, 847 from Rs. 13, 402 / to Rs. 43, 162 /. The High Court also dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue against the orders of the Tribunal. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) Section 24 B is a general provision applicable to all assessees except those who are liable to pay tax under the Act. It does not apply to any particular person or class of persons. [ 244 G ] (ii) The scheme of the Act shows that it is intended to provide for the recovery of taxes due from the deceased person and there can be no liability to tax in the hands of the heirs or legal representatives after his death. The provisions of section 24 A do not extend beyond the object for which they were enacted.

The petitioners were employed by the Andhra Pradesh State Government as Telephone Operators in the former Hyderabad State. They were appointed to the posts of Telephone Operators and Tele graphs, which are governed by the provisions of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. The petitioners contended that they had been appointed as Telephone Operator's on a temporary basis for a fixed period of one year without any break and that their appointments were made purely on temporary basis and not against permanent vacancies. The contention was rejected by this Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the appointment of the petitioners as Telephone Mechan ics under the Andhra State Government was not an appointment to a post or office within the meaning of Article 16 (3); (2) that the expression " any requirement " in section 3 of the Public Employment (Require ment as to Res idence) Act, 1957 means that the Central Government is empowered to make rules; and (3) that even if there was no provision in the Act empowering the Central government to make a rule prescribing the conditions of service of persons appointed to such posts, the power conferred by section 3 could be exercised only after consultation with the Governments concerned and not otherwise. Dismis sing the petitions, ^ HELD: (i) Section 3 of The Public Employment Act, 1955, does not confer any power upon the Central or the State Government to make any law prescribing the condition of employment or appointment to an office. It merely confers power on the Central and the State Governments to make Rules providing for the conditions subject to which such conditions may be prescribed. [ 128 C D ] (ii) The words'any requirement'cannot be read to warrant something which can have been said more specifically than its nature and content. The word'any'indicates that the power is given to Parliament to make laws. There is nothing in the language of the statute which requires that the words must be interpreted to mean what the legislature contemplated. If the intention of the Legislature was that the word'residence'should be construed as'residence ', then the use of the word " residence " would have been appropriate to include the time during which the person has to leave his place of residence. [ 129 E F ] (iii) The argument that the phrase'any required'should receive a restricted meaning and that the use in the latter part of the section must be taken to imply the use by the Central of the State of the same kind of residence in the State or Union territory, is not correct. The words " any condition " used in section 4 (3)( b) of the Act do not necessarily mean that the conditions mentioned therein are satisfied. The expression'any condition'in section 5 (1)( a) of that Act is wide enough to cover all the requirements of residence within the State. [ 130 B C ] (iv) The expression " residence in a particular part of a State " occurring in section 2 (3), when read in conjunction with the expression'residence in another part of India'in the context of the other clauses of section 3 (1), makes it clear that the term'residence within a Decision and Holding: Bench'in respect of the Bombay High Court at Hyderabad is wide and comprehensive enough to take in the matter of residence also. [ 131 G H ] (v) The definition of residence'in sub clause (3). of section 2 of the, is inclusive and not exhaustive.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898. He was tried by a Magistrate and convicted for offences under sections 52 and 52 of that Act. The High Court acquitted him on appeal but reduced his sentence to six months'rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the appellant had been in possession of the articles entrusted to him and therefore he could not be said to have secre ted them from the mere fact that they were found in the al mir ah which belonged to the father; (2) that the appellant was guilty of theft within the meaning of section 52 Of the Indian Penal Code because he did not take any part in the disposal of the article nor did he know what the number of articles he was keeping in his possession; (3) that there was no evidence to show that the articles seized from the house of the appellant belonged to him or that he had the opportunity to get at the articles examined by the police; and (4) that even if the articles were in the exclusive possession of his father he would not be guilty of criminal breach of trust. HELD: (i) The presumption arising under section 55 is rebut table and the onus shifts on the accused to prove that he has retained the articles with himself. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) It is well settled that unless the contrary is proved, the burden of proving that the accused has retained them is upon the prosecution. But where the presumption is one of law and the court can presume the existence of such facts as those mentioned in the Section. [ 35 C D ] (iii) If the presumption drawn by the court is reasonably capable of being rebutted by the accused by adducing evidence, the standard adopted by the courts below is that of a prudent man who would be in a position to establish that the possess or of the goods entrusted to the accused had the knowledge about them, is both probable and reasonable.

The appellant was convicted of contempt of court for disobedience of the order of the High Court dated December 20, 1963. He filed a petition in this Court under article 32 of the Constitution praying that he should be punished for committing contempt of the court by disobey ing its orders and that he may be directed to pay compensation to the State Government. The High Court dismissed his petition on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Courts have power to issue directions or writs for doing complete justice between the parties. [ 121 D ] (2) The power conferred upon the High Courts under Article 226 is not absolute but is subject to certain limitations. It is open to the High court to interfere if there is an error apparent on the face of the record. But where the impugned order is based on no evidence or mis reading of the documents or where the High is manifestly wrong such exercise of power will not be interfered with by this Court unless it is shown that there has been a manifest miscarriage of justice. [ 123 F H; 124 A B ] (3) There is no doubt that the High courts can interfere with the orders of subordinate courts only if they are shown to have acted within their jurisdiction or in excess of them as they think proper. The mere fact that the order passed by the High, Court is erroneous would not justify interference. [ 124 C E ] (4) The question whether the High'Court could interfere with an order of subordinate court when there is no error of jurisdiction committed by the subordinate court or there is a gross abuse of the process of the Court does not arise at all. [ 125 G ] (5) The object of section 50 is to prevent the Supreme Court from interfering with the administration of justice and to ensure that the rule of law prevail s. This Court has consistently held that the powers of the superior courts are not circum scribed by any specific provisions of the constitution. [ 126 F ] (6) The expression " due process of law " used in article 145 (3)( c) of the Con sti t ution means the rules of procedure applicable immediately before the commencement of the proceedings which are either expressly or by necessary implication applicable to the particular case. The word " due " in the context means " good faith ". [ 127 C ] (7) The word'due'in the first part of sub clause (b) of cl. (3), must be given its ordinary meaning. The words'due course of law'do not mean that the proceeding shall not be started ex parte. They con note that the party against whom action is taken is entitled to notice of the motion and to give reasonable time to the other side to represent and defend the case. If the party fails to show sufficient cause, the court may dismiss the suit.

The appellant was convicted of the murder of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) there was no evidence to show that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai; (2) that the extra judicial confession made by the appellant to Uj agar Singh was not admissible in evidence as he did not make any statement before the Police Officer at the time when the incident took place; and (3) that even if the extra Judicial confession of the accused is excluded from consideration, the fact that the recovery of the sword was made at the instance of the appro ver would not establish the case against the appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. HELD: (i) The extra judicial confessional statement of the Appellant recorded under section 164 Cr. P. C., cannot be relied upon for establishing guilt of the offence charged against him. It is well settled that a confession of a co accused is inadmissible in evidence unless it is corroborated either by other independent evidence or by other evidence. [ 211 E ] (ii) The confession of an accused person is not substantive evidence and can be used only to corroborate the evidence of the witness who has seen the crime and the commission of the crime. [ 212 A B ] (iii) The mere fact that a person is tried for an offence which is not punishable with death or with imprisonment for seven years does not amount to a confession within the meaning of section 24 of the Evidence Act. [ 213 D ] (iv) The fact that two persons were killed after the murder is not relevant under section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act because the former is not a direct evidence about the complicity of the third person in the crime but merely circumstantial evidence of his connection with the crime committed. The former is therefore admissible provided the circumstances from which such inference could be drawn are fully established. But where the prosecution relies upon the un corroborated testimony of the sole witness it is not safe to rely upon such un corroborated part of the evidence.

The petitioners, who were elected to the Municipal Committee in the election held in December 1978, filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the elections. They also challenged the validity and legality of the notification issued under Rule 4 (1) of the Rules on November 16, 1978 by which it was directed that the election should be held as per the schedule fixed for the election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have not given any cogent reasons why they did not consider the delay necessary to be condoned. It is well settled that when an order is quashed under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court has ample jurisdiction to interfere with the same if it finds that there is no sufficient cause for the non appearance of the petitioner before the Collector or he proceeded to pass an order dismissing the petition at the threshold. [ 10 31 C ] (ii) The power of the High court under Article 227 of the constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if it comes to the conclusion that the order passed by the Collector suffers from some illegality or infirmity, it can set aside the same in exercise of its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Con's titution. [ 32 G ] (iii) The mere fact that the Collector had taken action against the petitioners after the publication of the notice under Rule 5 (1), does not mean that the High Courts are debarred from exercising their power of judicial review in respect of orders passed by them. If the High courts do not come to the aid of those persons, it may turn out to be a case where the High Cour t has acted illegally or without jurisdiction.

The appellant was a director of the company. He was prosecuted under section 135 (1)( c) of the Companies Act, 1956 for failure to file the balance sheet and profit and loss account as required by section 134 (4). The trial court acquitted him but convicted him on appeal. On appeal the High Court held that the directors were guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 of the Indian Penal Code and directed their reinstatement with full back wages and continuity in service. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the directors under section 134 is not sustainable because they had been laid before the general body meeting and the general meeting was not convened. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) Section 134 (2) of 1913 Act provides that every person who fails to send a copy of the balance sheets and profit or loss account shall be liable to be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine or with both. [ 19 F ] (ii) The proviso to section 134 makes the position clear that if any person fails to call a general meeting he shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extent to two years or fine which may be imposed under section 76. It is not necessary that there should be a specific meeting. There must be a meeting of the general assembly at which the general meetings are to be called. If the general Meeting is not held, then the general notice of the meeting will have to be sent to the Registrar and the General Secretary. But where no such meeting has been held, the general decision would not be taken. [ 20 G H; 21 A B ] (iii) The requirement of section 134 cannot be complied with even though the general election is not set aside.

The appellant, a pro pr itor of a newspaper in the State of Hyderabad, was convicted by the Special Judge under section 5 (1)( d) of the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1950 for having published a pam ph let relating to the publication of news and views on certain matters concerning the public. He was sentenced to death and was also directed to pay a fine of Rs. 500 or in default further rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years'rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the provisions of article 14 were not applicable to the case; (ii) the procedure prescribed by the Act had not been followed; (iii) the trial should be held as bad because there was no evidence to show that the appellant had any reasonable apprehension of his guilt; and (iv) the appellant could not be convicted of an offence under section 3 of the Act. HELD: (Per H id ayat ullah C. J., Ray, Shah and Mud hol kar JJ.): Section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act is clear and unambiguous and does not suffer from any constitutional infirmity. It is not merely section 5 which provides that all offences punishable under the Act shall be tried by the special court constituted under section 9 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [ 298 G ] (ii). The object of the statute is to prevent the commission of crimes by persons who are not members of the police force and therefore it is necessary to see that they do not escape their clut ches. The fact that the legislature has made a distinction between cases of offences and classes of offences is irrelevant when considering whether the classification made is based upon some intelligible differentia having a rational relation with the object sought to be achieved. If the classification is reasonable then the question must be whether the differenti ation arises out of a difference in the circumstances of the matter which have a bearing on the question at issue.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service, and he was promoted to that post. He was later promoted as an Associate Professor of Radi other apy in the same college on January 9, 1963. On his promotion as a Reader in the Medical Department, he was posted at a place where he had been working for five years. In 1965, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of r. 8 (2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule of the Central Government Health Service Rules, 1966, which provided that " no person shall be entitled to claim seniority or selection unless he possesses the qualifications prescribed by these rules ". The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant was not holding the post of Professor in Orth opaed ics, he could not be considered to have been appointed as an Assistant Professor in Medicine and also because he did not hold the post in the Senior scale of pay. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression'in the absence of any qualification'in Rule 8 (2) means only'in accordance with the provisions of the rules '. [ 44 A B ] 2. The word'in'is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the sense of'in relation to the posts'and cannot be construed to mean'in regard to'the posts of Professor of Medicine in the concerned special ity. It is true that under the second proviso to rule 8 (2B), the expression'post'means the post which is included in the senior grade in the said service. But this would not make any difference when the post is shown to be a higher post than the post held by the incumbent. [ 45 G H; 46 3A C ] 3. The words'in addition'are wide enough to include the post mentioned in the first part of the definition. [ 47 F ] 4. The meaning of the word'post ', in the context of the present case, must depend upon the intention of the legislature. If the intention were to exclude the post from being treated as post in super time scale, then there would be no need to use the words'post '. The words " in the equivalent post'in clause (c) of sub section (2)( a) of Section 11 of the Act should be given their ordinary meaning. [ 46 E ] 5. The object of the second respondent who was admittedly holding the position of a Professor of radi ology in Maul ana Azad Medical College, Delhi, was to be considered for appointment to the post. The fact that the appellant had been appointed to the said post does not de tract from the fact that he was holding the said office in the Maul ana Shah Memorial Hospital. [ 48 D E ] 6. The letter dated February 25, 1967 issued by the Dean of the Maul ani Azad Medical University shows that the post was vacant and the appellant having been appointed in the former, he became eligible for appointment as a profess or in the department of the Ne ur ology. [ 49 E F ] 7. The appellant having become a Decision and Holding: Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, New Delhi, had the power to appoint him as Director in the General Duty Officer Grade II of the Indian Administrative Service. The post of Director General, Health Services, New Del h, was created in the year 1966. The posts of Director of Health Services were created in 1974. The next promotional post was the post reserved for the President of India. The recruitment rules made in 1970 provided for filling up of the post by direct recruitment. The relevant rules provide that the method of recruitment to the various posts specified therein shall be by direct appointment. The respondents were appointed as Research Officers in the Civil Hospital, New Y ork, and they were appointed in November, 1971.

The Company, which was a public limited company, had been carrying on business as manufacturers of paper and paper products. It entered into an agreement with the workmen for the payment of bonus at the rate of Rs. 75 per month in respect of each of the three categories of workers. In addition to this, it also agreed that the minimum wage payable by the Company would be Rs. 9. 60 per day. The dispute between the parties related to the fixation of wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, and the Tribunal made its award on the basis of the formula contained in the Agreement dated the 14th June, 1961. The Company contended before the Industrial Court that the basic wage should have been fixed at Rs. 90 per month instead of Rs 100 per month and that the Tribunal should have awarded Rs. 85 per month as bonus. The Industrial Tribunal held that the Company was entitled to claim only one month's basic wage and dearness allowance at the same rates as other paid employees. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that there was no justification for fixing the minimum wages at Rs 100 or Rs. 100 per mensem. The High Court further held that even if the Company could not pay more than what was being paid by the workmen, the total wage packet of the Company must be taken into account. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: (1) The basic wage is arrived at after taking into consideration the cost of living index, the cost price index, duration of production, station ary cost etc., and the profit and loss account. This has to be done keeping in view the general trend of industry, the infl ation rate, the amount of profits available, the capacity of the employer, the level of wages prevailing in the particular region, the general level of prices, the nature of the industry, number of units in the locality, the availability of raw materials, the depreciation allowed, the percentage of the profit earned, the over all development of the economy, the prospects of growth and the rise in the price of essential commodities. [ 10 D E ] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding that the entire wage packet was bound to go up to Rs. 84 per month. [ 11 C ] (3) The question whether the Tribunal was justified in awarding Rs. 80 per month on the basic wages was left open to be decided by the appropriate Government.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1959 60 on its total income. In the course of assessment proceedings under section 147 (1) and 148 (2), the Income tax Officer found that the assessee had concealed fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting year in question, income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for that year. He therefore issued a notice under section 148. The assessee appealed to the Commissioner who held that the order of the Income Tax Officer was not justified as he did not have reasons to believe that by reason of the omission or failure to disclose fully and fully all material information in his possession, the Income - tax Officer could not have issued a show cause notice under sections 148. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that it was a fit case for issue of a notice Under section 148; but the High Court set aside the order holding that there was no reason to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the Income. ate Tribunal. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Commissioner's order was not correct.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1943. It had a branch at Calcutta and its business consisted of two branches, one at Calcutta, another at Calcutta & Bombay and the other at Calcutta. In 1949 the appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the sale of certain shares of the said firm to be held by it on payment of Rs. 20 lakhs as commission. On August 1, 1948, the respondent issued a cheque for Rs. 38 lakhs towards the amount due under the said agreement. The cheque was dishonoured on presentation but the same was returned unpaid. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of the amount covered by the cheque. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the transaction was not one of'transfer of property within the meaning of section 25 (4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and dismissed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed both the suits. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant did not have any right to recover from the respondent the amount which he had paid to the appellant under the contract of partnership. [ 133 F ] (ii) The question whether there was a division or separate business carried on by the appellant does not arise because the business carried out by the respondent is one of the business es carried on at Calcutta where the appellant carries on his business. The business carried by him is one and indi visible and the business is carried on only at Calcutta; the business has been carried on in Calcutta since long. Therefore, the appellant cannot claim relief under section 25 of the Act. [ 134 C D ] (iii) The fact that the business of the appellant was taxed under the Act of 19 18 would not make any difference. The appellant could not be said to have acquired the business at all. If the business was carried on without the appellant's consent, then the appellant would be entitled to relief under the section.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the deceased, was the sole surviving member of the family. She had two sons and three daughters. The first son died in 1948 leaving behind his widow, her husband and four children. On his death she succeeded to the property left by him. After the death of her husband, the appellant filed an application under section 9 (1) of the Bombay Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 for partition of the joint family properties. The respondent contended that the appellant was not entitled to claim partition as he was not a coparcen er in the joint Hindu family and therefore, the partition effected between him and his brother was void. The High Court held that since the appellant had failed to prove that there was any partition of his joint family property, it could not be said that he was entitled to get the partition made. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) A partition may be either oral or registered. It is also well settled that if a partition takes place during the life time of a male member of a joint family, it would be binding on all members of the coparcen ary unless it is proved that the partition was made without his consent or without his knowledge or consent. [ 158 B C ] (ii) Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act provides that where a Hindu dies int estate, his interest therein shall devol ve according to the provisions of this Chapter on the date on which he mar ries succession thereto. Sub section (2) of section 6 provides that when a Hindu int estate has been divided among its several members, each member of such family shall become entitled to one such share. Under sub section (3), the shares of the heirs are to be ascertained on the basis of the birth of the separated male member who dies after the division. Therefore, the question whether the appellant became entitled to the share of the respondents in the property of the respondent does not arise. [ 159 F G; 160 E H ] (iii) The words " at the time of the partition " occurring in section 6 (1)( b) of Hindu Succession act include both the sons and daughters. If the intention of the legislature was to make the partition of a Hindu joint family governed by the Mit aksh ara law, then the same must have been done before the partition took place. But if the partition is not made immediately before the death, then it will be deemed to have been made only after the death in the eye of law. [ 161 D E ] (iv) The object of partition is to enable the members of a family to enjoy their respective rights in the coparcen ery property. When the partition takes effect after the lifetime of the father, the right of the daughter to inherit the property becomes absolute. The right of a female heir is not affected by the mere fact that the male holder acquires a vested interest in the family property.

The appellant Corporation was a statutory body constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Regulation of 1978. It was an autonomous Corporation established by and under the provisions of the State Act, called the Andhra University ి its affairs. The appellant was appointed as a full time sal ari ed employee in the Corporation on 1st September, 1956. He was appointed on 1st July, 1956 as a part time employee of the Corporation. On 1st September. 1956 he was appointed to the post of Manager (Personnel) with effect from 1st September 1956. In the year 1977 he was promoted as Manager (Finance). On 1 st October, 1956 his services were transferred to the Corporation and he joined the service of the corporation on 1st November, 1956 after completing the age of superannuation. On 31st January, 1976 he was re appointed as Manager in the corporation. On 30th April, 1979 he was again appointed as an Assistant Manager in a Corporation which was taken over by the Corporation w. e. f. 1st September,. 1956. On the same day he was also appointed as manager in the Central Government. On 9th June, 1979 the appellant was re employed as Manager's on a temporary basis for a period of one year without any break. On 15th February, 1979, the appellant made a representation against his termination of his service before the Central Govt., but the Central Govern ment did not take any action thereon. Thereafter, the Corporation passed an order terminating his services on 8th March, 1979. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned order was violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as it had been passed without affording an opportunity of hearing to the appellant. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the President under Clause (3) of Article 311 is a very wide power. It is not intended to be exercised arbitrarily or capric iously. It has to be used sparingly and only in cases where the interest of public justice demands interference. [ 10 31 C ] 2. The object of the regulation is to prevent vested interests being affected. The regulations are framed for the benefit of the employees of the Corporations. The Regulations have been framed in exercise of powers under Section 43 of the A. P. Municipal Corporations Act, 1949. The Regulation provides for the constitution of a Corporation consisting of three members. The first proviso to clause (c) of sub section (2) of Section 11 empowers the Central government to make rules for regulating the conditions of service of officers and other employees of such corporations. Sub section (4) of section 11 provides that the Central Board shall consist of a Chairman and two other members to be appointed by the Central Gover nment. The Central Government may appoint a person to be the Chairman of the Board. The appointment of the Chairman is subject to the approval of the Central Gov er nment. Under the proviso to sub section 2 (b), the Central Go ver nment can appoint a Chairman who will be a member of the Executive Committee if there is no other member present at the meeting. The Decision and Holding: Secretary of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, dated 21st March, 1963 shows that the Board was formed in accordance with the provisions contained in Chapter IV of the Act. The relevant portion of the Regulation reads as follows: " The Central Govt. shall constitute a Standing Committee consisting of the representatives of the employers and the employees representing them. The number of persons so nominated shall not exceed six. The Chairman shall be ex officio Chairman of these Standing Committees. The Committee shall meet at least once every quarter. The quorum of the meeting shall be five." The question whether the Standing Committee should be constituted or not would depend upon the terms of the agreement between the parties. The Standing Committee consists of 5 members.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and belonged to the State cadre. He was appointed as a Judge in 1963. On his appointment he was promoted as an Additional District Judge on February 12, 1975. In January 1974 he was transferred from Delhi to Jammu & Kashmir. On March 2, 1976 he was posted as Chief Justice of the Punjab High Court. On April 16, 1975 he was appointed a Judge of the High Court as a Special Judge under section 19 (3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On May 1, 1975 the President of India issued a notice to him stating that the Government had decided to remove him from his office with immediate effect. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice did not amount to contempt of court. It also held that the letter was not a public notice. Allow ing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The notice was defective. The notice merely stated that " it is proposed to remove you from your office ". The notice did state that if you do so then you will be removed from his post. The question whether any publication was intended for the purpose of taking action against you would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 247 C ] The notice dated December 9, 1975 clearly states that the appellant was asked to show cause why he should not be removed. The respondent replied to the notice but did not respond. The letter does not say anything about the personal views or suggestions given by the Judges. The reason is obvious. The letters written by the appellant were clear. They did not mention what particular portions of the letter were. The words used are " may feel conf ident's ", " may think or thought fit ". The letter was addressed to the Chief Justice only. There was no reference to the letter. The Chief Justice wrote the letter to the President. The contents of the said letter indicate that the Chief Jus tices were requested to look into the matter personally. The President of the Bar Association recommended that the letters be sent to the Registrar General of the Supreme Court. The Governor of Haryana wrote to the Secretary of the Chief Minister's Office requesting him to send copies of the letters received by the Chief Ministers. The copy was forwarded to the Advocate General. The Secretary wrote back saying that the Superintendent of the Court should come to know of the contents of this letter. A copy of the communication was also sent to him. The Vice Chancellor of the University refused to take notice of the fact that the information contained in the letter dated November 6, 1975 was not supplied. The Registrar informed the Bench that the Registrar was directed to supply the information. The order was challenged by the appellants by filing a Writ Petition in the High. Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts have power to interfere with orders passed by them. The power of judicial review conferred on the High courts under Article 226 of the Constitution is confined to cases where there is an error apparent on the face of the record.

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Income tax Investigation Commission. He was charged with offences under section 5 (1) and section 6 (2) of the Act for having failed to carry out assessment proceedings in respect of his income, profits and gains. The investigation revealed that he had concealed certain material facts from the Income Tax Department and had not disclosed them in his return. On the basis of the information obtained by him, the Income tax Officer issued notice to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be prosecuted for an offence under section 34 of the Income - tax Act. The petitioner submitted his explanation which was considered by the Commission and the Commission passed its order on December 31, 1954. The Commission held that there was no evidence against the petitioner and accordingly discharged him. The State Government appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The provisions of section 5 of the impugned Act were discriminatory as they did not apply to persons proceeded against under the Indian In com et ax Act; (ii) the procedure prescribed by the impugned statute was more drastic than the procedure laid down by the Indian Penal Code and the principles of natural justice were violated; (iii) the petitioner's case was governed by the provisions of the [ Indian Income Tax Act ] and the proceedings before the Commission could not be said to be vitiated merely because the petitioner was asked to submit his explanation. The fact that the petitioner had been called upon to explain his case would not make any difference since the procedure contemplated by section 34 Of the Indian Act was not followed.

The appellant Association was registered as a " commercial establishment " under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had been carrying on business in various parts of India and it carried on several other activities including that of conducting sales, exhibition s, selling or otherwise dealing in certain commodities. In respect of its business activity, it filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of section 2 (5) of the Act which provided for exemption from registration of any trade or business.

The appellant was the owner of an estate. He had a right to receive and recover rent from its predecessor in title, but he did not have any right to claim it as his own property. The income tax authorities held that the amount received by him as pension was not taxable under section 4 (3)( viii) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the payment was not exempt from taxation as income under section 4A (1) of Income tax law. The fact that the assessee had been granted a pension for a period of 20 years would not make him liable to pay income tax. The amount was not taxed because the appellant had no right to it. It was not therefore taxable as income. The question whether the amount was taxable or not was a matter which could be decided only after evidence was led. The appellant's contention that the sum was not agricultural income is without substance. The character of the receipt depends upon the nature of the payment and the circumstances in which it is made. The payment may be regarded as a payment in instalments of the value of the property leased out. If the payment is made in instalments, the character of payment cannot be determined on the basis of what the parties say at the time when they entered into the transaction. In the present case there was nothing to show that the appellant was receiving any income from the estate. The payments were made in installments. The amounts were paid in instalments. The mere fact that there was a settlement between the appellant and the respondent does not mean that the money was not income.

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were promoted as Charg emen Grade II on the basis of their seniority as Supervisors'A '. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the promotion of the respondents to the post of Chargeman Grade I and prayed for quashing the order dated 2nd February, 1981 passed by the Director General of Ordnance Factories, Madhya Pradesh, Bhopal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the promotion was not made on the recommendation of the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 8 (1) of the Central Industrial Security Force Rules, 1966. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to be given the same relief which they had claimed in the writ petitions before the Madhya Pradesh High Court. [ 107 E ] 2. In view of the fact that the appellants in the instant case have been given the benefit of the principle of " equal pay for equal work ", it is not a fit case for initiating any proceedings for contempt again st the respondents. [ 108 G H ] 3. The impugned judgment of the High court is set aside and the writ appeals are dismissed.

The appellant, a private operator of the State Transport Undertaking, filed applications before the Tribunal for grant of permits on various routes in the State. The Tribunal held that the application was not maintainable and directed the State Government to consider the same. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (i) since the proviso to section 63 (7) is independent of the rule making power conferred upon the Central Government under section 68 F (1), it is not open to the Tribunal to give its own interpretation; (ii) the proviso does not confer any arbitrary or excessive power on the Tribunal but only en sures that the rules are made for the purpose of giving effect to the scheme; and (iii) the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain an application for approval of the scheme unless it is satisfied that the conditions laid down in the proviso are fulfilled. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The proviso to sub section (3) of section 63 is valid and intra vires. [ 10 31 B ] (2) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction in the matter to interfere with the order of the Regional Transport Authority granting the permit. It could not have been challenged because the Tribunal had not given any finding as to whether the conditions imposed were reasonable or not. [ 11 C D ] (3)( a) The word " may " occurring in section 43 (1 A) means " shall be deemed to be prescribed ". The words " such other conditions as may be prescribed " in the first part of the said sub section mean " such conditions as the State may impose ". The expression'such other condition'in the second part of section 43 E (1)( b) means that the provisions of Chapter IV A are applicable to all operators except those who are entitled to the benefit of the schemes. [ 12 G H ] (4) The expression " other conditions " in section 63 cannot be read to mean that the Rules must be framed for the purposes of giving preference to persons whose names are entered in the list maintained under section 63.

The respondent, a registered dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, was assessed to sales tax for the assessment years 1948 49 and 1949 50. On October 5, 1956 he filed a petition under section 19 of the Act claiming that the transactions in question were not liable to be taxed as they were not entered into by him with the State Government at all. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the transaction was one of sale of goods and hence taxable under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the impugned deed of transfer did not create any legal fiction or make it an act binding on the transferor; (2) that there was no transfer of property within the meaning of section 10 of the Indian E ase ments Act, 1882, and therefore the provisions of the said Act were not applicable to the case; (3) that even if the transferee had been assessed to tax under the provisions Of the Act, the liability could not be fastened upon the transferee unless the transfer was made by him; (4) that since the transfer of business was effected before April 1, 1948, the same was governed by the provisions contained in section 19 (2)( c) of the Madras Act IX of 1939 which provided that " where a registered instrument has been executed before the date of its execution, then, notwithstanding anything contained in such instrument, but save as otherwise provided in sub section (1), such instrument shall have effect as if it were an instrument referred to in section 17 of the principal Act." Held, that the contention of the appellant must fail. Section 19 (1)( b) of Madras Act No. I of 1959 provides that every transfer of immovable property is subject to the other provisions of that Act. It does not apply to transfers effected by a person who carried on the business immediately before the relevant date. The object of the provision is to prevent evasion of tax by transferring properties belonging to persons other than the transferor to others. The purpose of the section is to enable the transferee to recover from the transferor the amount outstanding on the date when the transfer took place. The proviso to section 19 makes it clear that the transferee will have to pay the arrears of sales tax due by the transferor only after the transfer is completed. The words'until the whole of the amount remaining unpaid'are wide enough to include the liability created by the transfer.

The respondent was a Government servant. He was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Police, Bombay State on February 2, 1955. On appeal to the Inspector - General of Prisons, Gujarat State, he was suspended and later reinstated in service. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the order of dismissal was not one of punishment but of removal; (2) that the order did not amount to a penalty within section 60 (2)( b) of the Act as it related to a contract within the meaning of section 61 (2); and (3) that there was no breach of article 311 of the Constitution because the order was passed without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The High Court had rightly held that the appellant's claim for arrears of salary was not barred under section 60 of the Bombay Re organisation Act 1960. [ 810 B ] (ii) There is nothing in section 60 or section 61 which makes any distinction between " loss of pay or wages " and " other monetary benefit ". It is true that the word " any " does not mean money or profit. But what is important is that the person who has been dismissed should be entitled to compensation either in whole or in part. If the termination of his services is wrongful, then the question arises whether the dismissal amounts to a forfeiture of his entire past service. [ 811 G H ] (iii) The words " cease " are wide enough to include something more than " cessation of employment " and do not refer to a mere incident of a contract. The word " cease ", therefore, must be given its ordinary meaning. The expression " cease to be a member of the service " means an act done by a public servant in the course of his employment. A break in service occurs when a public officer is absent and the period of absence is treated as leave without pay. [ 812 C D ] (iv) The word'cease'in section 61 refers to the termination by the employer of the employee during the period the service remains with him. The words'cease to serve'have reference to the time during which the employee is absent. The phrase'cease ', according to Web ster's Dictionary, means'to cease '. In common parlance, however, the word'ceases'may mean'cease '. The word is used in the context of the word,'cease '; and'cease is defined in section 2 (p). The word ceases'means to cease after the day on which it is made. The term'cease implies the cessation of the work. Therefore, if the work is terminated before the expiry of the term, the workman becomes a'workman '. [ 813 E F ] (v) The definition of'ceased'in the case of a temporary employee is inclusive of the period during which he is absent, while the word is not used in section 62 of the Indian Penal Code, it is clear that the same includes anything done by way of resignation or otherwise. [ 814 E F ].

The appellant was a lessee of coal mine in the suit land. He leased out to the respondents, and took possession of the same on November 23, 1905. On June 15, 1941, he applied for the grant of a lease under section 3 (1) of the Indian Mines Act, 1923, which was granted by the Deputy Commissioner on October 11, 19 24. Under this lease the appellants were required to remove coal from the encroached area within three years of the date of the expiry of the lease. The appellants claimed that they had been wrongfully prevented from removing coal from their lands and that the entire period of limitation should be computed from the date when they became entitled to possession of such coal. The trial court held that the appellants'claim was barred by limitation but dismissed the suit. In appeal to the High Court it was contended: (i) that the suit was not barred by time; (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the plaintiffs had knowledge of the alleged encroachment only in the year 1932 and that if the period of two years had elapsed the suit would have been filed after the expiry thereof; (iii) that even if the boundary line between the two estates is divided into two parts, the boundary of the leasehold property could not exceed three years as provided in cl. (b) of s. 2 of the Regulation; (iv) that since the appellants had obtained an order of injunction against the respondent restraining him from removing the coal from his encroached portion, the suit must fail; and (v) that in any event the suit having been based on the title of the appellants, the plaint was not maintainable. Held, that the question whether the suit had been properly valued for the purposes of court fee and jurisdiction does not depend upon the correctness of the valuation or the nature of the suit or the relief claimed. It is well settled that where the plaintiff has no right to sue, he cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. He was suspended from service on account of an industrial dispute pending before it and he was dismissed by the company. On appeal, the Industrial Tribunal held that the termination of his services was not bona fide and that there was no evidence to show that he had been guilty of misconduct or bad conduct which led to the termination. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant's contention that the employer could have proceeded under section 33 is correct but the question whether the employer can now press his right purely on contract and say that under the contract he has unfettered right to hire and fire his employees cannot be answered because the employer did not want to take action under such a rule. [ 830 E ] (2) There is nothing more to be said and that the decision of this case is also inapplicable to the present case. [ 832 A B ] (3) The fact that the appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication shows that there were no other considerations which justified the conclusion that the impugned order was mala fide or was a colourable exercise of power.

The appellant, a tenant of a building in which a cinema theatre was situate, filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure for leave to amend the written statement and also to file additional written statement. The Trial Court dismissed the application on the ground that it had no power to grant any amendment or alter the pleadings at the stage of evidence. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the order did not fall within the scope of section 115 (1) of the Act and set aside the order of the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order passed by the Trial Judge is final and conclusive between the parties to a suit. [ 442 E ] (ii) The question whether a party has been able to establish a case decided by a Court subordinate to the High court can be raised before the Appellate Court if there is an adjudication by the Court with regard to the rights of the parties in controversy arising out of the agreement dated November 27, 1954. [ 444 B C ] (iii) The expression " case " as an entire proceeding means all proceedings connected with the dispute in such a way as to show what kind of relief the parties are entitled to. If the parties have already adduced evidence before the Trial court, then the trial court will have to decide the matter in accordance with law. [ 445 D F ] (iv) The word'case'in section 115 does not mean that the whole proceeding is to be tried only by the trial judge. It is only when the trial is complete and the judgment is pronounced that the decision of the trial Court would be final. [ 446 G H;

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the State of Uttar Pradesh on contract basis. He was appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer by order dated 30. 8. 1985. On his appointment, he was given an extension of service upto 30th August, 1985. In the meanwhile, the respondent was allowed to continue in service till 30th of August, 2 1985. However, the appellant issued a show cause notice dated 29. 3. 1988 stating that the respondent had not extended his period of service beyond 30th of Aug., 1985 and no orders were passed on the said notice. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated 26. 7. 1988. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the termination of services of the respondent could not be sustained because it did not amount to a contract which specified the term of his appointment which extended only up to 30th of July, 1985 unless there was a further extension of his period. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of termination of service served on the respondent is entitled to remain in service until he completed the age of 58 years. [ 245 B ] 2. The impugned order of the High court setting aside the order of reinstatement of the Respondent with effect from 30. 08. 1985 cannot be sustained. It is on this ground alone that the order was set aside. [ 246 E F ] 3. The judgment of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court dated 24. 3, 1988 is set aside and the order passed on review on 26. 07. 1988 is restored. [ 247 C D ] 4. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence of life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment for life. On an application made by the State against the order of acquittal, the Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence on the ground that there were no reasonable grounds for believing that the deceased had been assaulted by the accused with a knife. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no rule of thumb that where the evidence is clear and unambiguous, no question of reading ver ses the language used can arise. But it is only when the witness is absolutely clear in his mind that he would not have been able to recognise the assailants or any one of them. [ 271 C D ] (2) It is true that if two reasonably probable and even ly balanced views of the evidence are possible, one must necessarily conced e the existence of a reasonable doubt. But, fan ci ful and remote pos sibilities must be left out of account. To entitle an accused person to the benefit of any doubt arising from the possibility of a du ality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him. If two reasonably possible and reasonable conclusions can be reached on the basis of such evidence, the benefit must go to the accused. [ 272 E H;

The appellant was appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court and he was posted in the High Court.
