He was convicted for an offence under section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by the Special Judge, Delhi on the ground that he had committed offences punishable under sections 161 and 165 I. P. C. and section 5 1 6 I. A. S. Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. On appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) Section 5 (1)( e) of the Act is not applicable to the present case because the appellant was not holding any office at the time when the alleged offence took place; (ii) the sanction given by the President of India under article 124 (4) of Constitution was only a recommendation or approval of the Governor General who could not be said to have been granted without the aid of the Council of Ministers; (iii) the order of removal from service passed against him was invalid since no reasons were recorded therein for his dismissal from service; and (iv) the appellant's services were terminated after being found guilty of misconduct and having failed to satisfy the requirements of Article 311 (2). Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The provisions of clause (e) are intended to provide for one of the three well known methods of disciplinary action which must be followed by courts while dealing with the question of punishment. [ 10 31 B ] (2)( i) It is true that the language used in clauses (e), (f) and (g) of sub section (1), namely, " shall be competent to impose upon any person who is a member of a Civil Service of the Union or of a State, a right to hold office during the pleasure of the President or the Governor of a covenant ing State, and such other powers as may be necessary for the proper discharge of its functions." In the instant case, there was nothing to show that the appellant had any connection with the independence of the judiciary. There was no evidence to show how the appellant could have access to the independence power of the higher judiciary. [ 32 G H ] (3) The fact that the Judges of the High Courts and the Supreme court were chosen as judges of the high judicial wing of the Government of India would not make them part of the administrative machinery of the State. If they did not do so, then the High court should have dismissed the writ petition. But if the High courts were to exercise their jurisdiction over the subordinate judiciary, then, the High Cour thas to see whether the decision of the Chief Justice of the country to which the appellant belonged was taken bona fide or not. [ 33 D E ] (4)( a) The expression " civil judge " has been defined in section 2 (d) of Act, 1952. That definition includes all persons who have pecuniary interest in any contract or employment with the Central Government or the State Government. The word " employee " has also been defined to mean any person employed for wages in or in connection with any industrial, commercial or industrial undertaking or Decision and Holding: an office of profit under the Central or State Government or a local authority. The definition does not include persons who are employed in connection With the affairs of the Central Industrial Security Force. [ 34 F G ] (b) The words " civil servants " occurring in section 5 are wide enough to include persons employed in the armed forces of the state but not workmen in the sense of the term " officers ". The expression'civil servant'is not confined to those who are serving in connection or whose duty is directly or indirectly connected with the affairs and business of the Indian Armed Forces. The expression includes persons employed for purposes of private profit.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. He belonged to the scheduled caste group of Sun ri, but he belonged to a Scheduled Caste. On the death of his father in 1965, the appellant and his mother were members of that caste. In 1956, they had been converted into Hindu ism by which their families were divided into two classes, one class and another class. They were not Hindus. The appellant's case was that there was no evidence to show that the appellant belonged to any other community or tribe as claimed by him. The Tribunal held that the evidence showed that the appe l l ant belonged to " the same caste group ". It also found that the witnesses who gave evidence on behalf of the appellant did not say that the other two castes were different from those mentioned in item 40. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant against this decision. Held: (i) The appellant is not entitled to claim that the election of the respondent should be set aside because it was established that the respondent's caste was included in the list of backward classes. [ 931 B ] (ii) The evidence clearly shows that the tribunal came to the conclusion that the question whether the appellant belongs to the Scheduled Caste was really a question of fact and could have been properly considered by the Tribunal if it was otherwise within its jurisdiction. The finding of the Tribunal that the failure to establish that the person whose caste was assigned was not a Scheduled caste was perverse. There was nothing to show when the tribunal went wrong in coming to the said conclusion. The evidence before the Tribunal was not sufficient to prove that the caste of the first respondent was included among the other than those specified in item 39.

The appellant, a tenant of the flat in dispute, was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 18 (1)( b) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947. He filed an appeal to the Sessions Judge against his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed his appeal but reduced the fine to Rs. 30, 000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the term " relinquishment " is not defined in the Transfer of Property Act; (ii) the word " relinquishment ", as used in section 19 (2) of that Act, means relinquishment of a right or interest in property made after the execution of the conveyance; and (iii) the expression " relinquishment of tenancy " must be construed according to its gram matical meaning. HELD: (1) A transfer of a lease by a tenant does not come within the definition of'relinquishment '. It is only when there is no transfer of any right of occupation by the landlord that he can be said to have surrendered possession of the premises. [ 108 E F ] (2)( a) The words " assignment " and " relinquishment are not sy non y mous terms. They do not mean that they are sy non's enti ent or integrated concepts. They are sy ru ps es which may be associated with one another. They refer to two distinct and different situations. The former is a case where the lessee has parted with possession of a flat without receiving consideration for the same. But if the transferee pays the price therefor, the latter is a lessee. If the transferee fails to pay the price due from him, the transferee will be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and this liability is contr ac t arily attached to the transferor who holds his interest. [ 109 C D ] (3) The word " surrender " occurring in section 18 of the Transfer Of Property Act includes relinquishment of the tenancy by a transferee. The word'relinquishment'is not sy Non usual. It is a concept of relinquishment. It con notes relinquishment of rights. It refers to relinquishment of interest. It also refers to the relinquishment of leasehold interest. In the present case, the deed of transfer dated 1st December, 1948, shows that the transfer of the lease by the original lessor was not a grant nor was it a mere transfer of lease by sub lease or otherwise. Therefore, the transfer by the transferee was not void. [ 110 H; 111 A B ] (4) The transfer of possession by a lessee or a lessee of his interests in the suit property cannot be regarded as a gift or exchange. The fact that the lessee had transferred the lease to the plaintiff did not make any difference since the transfer was not by way of a covenant. The transfer was by a deed. The document merely rec ites that the transferee had agreed to transfer the lease. The intention of the parties was that the transferor should convey the title to the transferee. There is nothing in the language of the section which suggests that such a transfer would amount to a transfer of interest in immovable Decision and Holding: (5) The object of the provision is to prevent evasion of tax. The legislature has clearly provided for the penalty of fine and imprisonment. [ 112 G H; 113 A B ].

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1960. It had a factory at village Kh or adi, Taluka Ch ory asi, District Bharuch, Gujarat State. In the year 1961 there were two factories of the appellant and one at village Bh am ara. The factory was closed on March 31, 1963. On December 22, 1963 the appellant filed an application under section 33 (1) (b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for revising the wage scales and dearness allowance to be paid to its employees. The Tribunal rejected the said application holding that it was not justified in law as it was bound by the decision taken by the Government of India in respect of revision of pay scales and other service conditions of the workmen. The appellant challenged the award before this Court by special leave. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the appellant is entitled to revise the wage scale with effect from January 1, 1978 has to be determined in accordance with the principles laid down in the Act. [ 133 C ] 2. The object of the Act is to provide gratuity to workmen who are employed in industrial establishments. The Act provides for payment of gratuity to all workmen except those who have been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with an industrial dispute pending before any authority constituted under the Act, while Section 33 B provides for the grant of certain benefits to workmen. Section 33 A provides that no workman shall be required to work in any industrial establishment unless he has completed six months'continuous service in that establishment. Section 25 E provides that where any workman is entitled, without complying with the provisions of section 25 F, to payment of compensation which shall not exceed three months'wages, the employer shall pay to every employee a sum equal to his average monthly wages for each wage period not exceeding five thousand rupees, and in the case of a workman employed in a seasonal industry during the preceding ten months, the wages of such workman shall not be less than twice the average monthly earnings of the last six months computed under sub section (1). [ 133 H; 134 A B ] 3. The expression " industrial establishment " occurring in section 2 (13) of Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 means any industrial undertaking specified in the Schedule thereto. The definition of " industrial dispute " in section 3 (k) includes only disputes relating to matters referred to in Chapter V of the I. D. Act. The term " industrial disputes " is defined in section 4 (k), but does not include a dispute between an individual workman and an employer. The word " industrial " is generally used in the sense of a trade or business carried on by an individual or a group of individuals. The words " industrial concern " and " industrial undertaking " are defined in the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Rules, 1946, and they are so mentioned in the schedule annexed to the rules. Rule 1 of the said Rules provides that the number of persons employed in an industrial establishment shall be one hundred and twenty times the number employed therein. Rule 2 (g) defines " industrial employment " thus: " Industrial Establishment " means Decision and Holding: Industrial Establishment. (i) A person employed in any industry in an industry immediately connected with the industry concerned may be called a representative union if he belongs to any of the following classes, namely: (a) a member of an industrial staff; (b). a member or members of any other union; (c) a labour union; Explanation II. An " industrial worker " means a member who is employed mainly in a managerial capacity but does include a member Of any All India Service of Employees (not being a Member of any All ocation of Employees) ". The above definition shows that the term " employee " is wide enough to include a person who is directly employed in the industry.

The appellant company was awarded a contract for the supply of cotton to its workmen. The respondent company paid wages at the rate of Rs. 1, 000 per month and the appellant company filed an application under section 15 (2) of the Payment of Wages Act, which was dismissed by the Labour Court on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim made by the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Bombay High Court has rightly held that the powers conferred on the Industrial Tribunal under the Act are not limited to making awards in respect of matters covered by the terms of the contract between the parties but they do not extend to those cases where the term of the agreement is expressed or implied from the terms thereof. [ 423 C D ] (ii) The power conferred by section 2 (vi) is subject to the limitations contained in the first part of section 23 (1) of which the words " any award made by an industrial tribunal shall be final ". It is true that the word'may'in section 2 of the Act does not mean that the power conferred upon the Industrial Tribunals by the Act is confined only to making an award or decision as contemplated by the said provision. But if the intention of the legislature was to exclude the power of the Industrial tribunals to make new contracts between the employer and the employees, then there would have been no necessity for enacting a separate provision like section 2, sub section (vi), which provides that every such award shall be deemed to be a contract between both the parties. [ 424 G H; 425 A B ] (iii) Section 2 (v) of Act defines the term " award " as meaning " an interim or final determination of any question relating to the existence, effect or validity of an agreement between the employers and the workman concerned in any matter connected with the dispute in which the agreement relates. The expression " award includes an interim award " in the definition clause is wide enough to include an award made in pursuance of a settlement or award arrived at by a tribunal. [ 426 E F ] (iv) The object underlying the amendment of section 2 is to enable the Government to appoint as many persons as it thinks fit to assist the arbitrator in the disposal of his disputes. The purpose of the amended definition is to provide for the appointment of arbitrators and to give them certain additional powers. The object of the amendment is to remove doubts about the nature of the original arbitration proceedings and to provide that the new contract will continue to govern the relations between the Parties until a fresh contract between them is entered into.

The appellant was a public servant, and the prosecution against him was for an offence under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. He was convicted by the trial court but acquitted on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that sanction was not necessary as the case had been investigated into by the police and no sanction was required under section 197 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held: (i) That sanction is necessary when there is a prima facie case or where the investigation in the course of the same transaction substantially affects the merits of the accusation made against the accused person; (ii) that the facts alleged constitute the offences mentioned in section 409 are such as would justify the issue of a search warrant against the appellant and that the sanction must be given by the officer who actually investigated the case; and (iii) that if the facts stated in the sanction show that the object of the official was dishonest or fraudulent, then sanction could not be given unless the facts disclosed disclose an offence which he committed.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. For the assessment years 1949 47 and 1950 51 the Income Tax Officer treated the profit or loss of the assessee as business in British India and added Rs. 79, 275 as the amount of profits and gains attributable to the business during the two accounting years ending on 31 2 1949 and 1951 respectively. On appeal by the assessee it was contended that (i) the words " any person " occurring in section 10 would include a firm carrying on business in an Indian State; (ii) that the word " such " in section 24 (1) means only " any one whose total income is included in the total income of the previous year ". Held: (i.) Section 32 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, which provided that the aggregate of the profits and losses arising from all sources shall not be included in computing the total world income of a previous year of a Hindu undivided family, did not exclude the operation of section 10 of the Act. (ii). Under section 32 (1)( b) of the Travancore Income tax and Sur charge Act, 1946, the expression'business'in section 2 (13) meant business in the Indian State and so could not be said to apply to the case where the business in Travancore State was carried on in the territories of the former Indian State. (iii) The proviso to section 24 of the Ex cess Prof its Tax Act, 1940, applied to the facts of the present case because the word'business ', in section 32, had been used in the sense of business in Part A of the First Schedule to the Indian Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. It had a factory at Bombay and it was carrying on business of manufacturing, engineering, production and sale of all products including paper and paper. In the years 1953 and 1954 the appellant company entered into agreements with its employees for fixing the age of retirement at 60. The workmen were paid their dues by the respondent Company as well as by the appellant Company. On December 31, 1954, the appellant filed an application under section 33 (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, before the Labour Court, Delhi, praying that the Tribunal should fix the age at 55 or 60. This application was dismissed by the Tribunal but the High Court allowed the application holding that the question raised by the Union did not fall within the scope of the reference made to it under section 10 (1)( d) of this Act. Hence the appeal by special leave. Held: (i) The words " generally applicable to any particular industry " occurring in section 2 (k) of that Act mean " generally prevalent or anticipated ". The expression " ordinarily applicable " is defined in section 4 (6) of which it is clear that the normal rule of thumb that no employee shall be retired after he has attained the age unless it appears to have been determined on an examination of his record of service by a competent authority; (ii) when an employer who has always been willing to employ labour has not been able to prove that he had ever been employed in connection with the affairs of the industrial concern during such time, then the question whether the conclusion recorded by the tribunal that the employee's previous finding regarding the age could be regarded as conclusive would not arise.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961. It had a large stock of raw materials, machinery and plant, including fer til iser, chemicals etc., which were to be supplied by it to M / s. L. A. Mit che ll Ltd. On May 19, 1965 the appellant company entered into an agreement with M / S. L ee & Co. for supply of machinery and equipment. In June 1965 the company executed a formal agreement with the Ger man company whereby the latter agreed to supply certain machinery and equipments to the company at its cost. The agreement also provided that the company would take over the management of the company from the first respondent's company. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of Rs. 4, 80, 000 as damages on account of breach es committed by them. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant could not have been compelled to enter into any contract with the company because of the alleged fraud or mis feas ance on the part of the respondents. [ 340 C ] (2) The conduct of the appellant is such that he cannot be held liable for the acts of the directors of the Company. [ 342 E ] (3) The fact that the appellant did not execute the collabor ation agreement with L. a. Mit sub ishi does not make him liable for any damage caused to the property. He has no right whatsoever to recover possession of the machinery from the company. [ 343 G ] (4) The question whether the appellant can be said to have acted dishonestly or fraudulently to obtain the benefit of the contract between the parties is a matter which must be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 344 B ] (5) The principle underlying section 23 of the Indian Contract Act applies only where there is a clear intention to create legal rights or obligations or liability arising out of a contract. If the person who has signed the document is guilty of a criminal offence, the court will not permit him to do so. [ 345 F ] (6) The object of the agreement is to protect the interest of the creditors and to prevent the creditor from committing breach of his obligations under the contract. The object is to see that the debtor is protected from the penalty imposed by law. [ 346 D ] (7) The purpose of the resolution is to ensure that the workers are paid their dues without demur or other charges. The scheme of the Act is to enable the workmen to get the work done through the firm. The legislature has given the power to the Board to decide whether the work should be done through one agency or through another. The power conferred upon the Board is subject to the conditions laid down in section 237 (b). The power to appoint a committee is not dependent on the existence of a written agreement between the employer and the employee. The Committee appointed by the Government has to perform its duties and functions. The powers of the Committee are limited to the determination of the terms of reference made by the Board. [ 347 H;

The appellant was convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that he had been falsely implicated in a dacoity case, as no offence was committed at all. HELD: (i) The conviction is correct but it must be held that there was no evidence against him. [ 536 B ] (ii) There is nothing in the evidence to show that the appellant was in any way concerned with the crime or that he was a receiver of stolen property from some other person who was not even mentioned in the F. I. R. In the circumstances, the sentence of three years'rigorous imprisonment will meet the ends of justice in this case. [ 537 C D ] (iii) The sentence of two years'imprisonment would meet the end of justice if the appellant were to be acquitted.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the provisions of the, and had been carrying on business in certain commodities. He was convicted by the trial court for offences under section 5 (2) read with section 11 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court dismissed his petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notification and its application were invalid because: (i) there was no specification of the substance as poison; (ii) the notification did not state that the substance should be declared as poison for the entire country; and (iii) the State Government could not have issued any such notification without specifying the particular article or names of the articles which would come within the purview of the Act. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The notification and the application of the relevant rules do not require the same to be specified in the notification. It is only necessary that the same substance should also be declared to be poison for purposes of the enactment. [ 225 C ] (2). The notification does not require that the particular substances mentioned therein should be notified as poison. The notification merely states that the specified substances are to be treated as poison if they are " poison ed ". The word'poison'has been defined in section 2 (x) of Act. The words'poison ','poison ing'and'adulter ated'are defined in the Act as'poison '. The definition of poison given in section 3 (x), therefore, cannot be applied to the present case. [ 226 F G ] (3) Section 2 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, provides that the word'po isons'means poison used either by one person or by another in the presence of other persons. The word " po isons " in section 5 includes po isons. The term po isons is wide enough to include po isons which can be termed but not poison. [ 227 E H ] (4) The word po isons must be construed in its wid est sense so as to take in po isons other than po isons and containing par ce ls and cor respon ds to po isons mentioned in clauses (x). A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This limitation is unreasonable or off ends the petition ers'right to carry on the same. No question of discrimination arises in such circumstance.

The assessee, a partnership firm carrying on business of money lending and other allied goods, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act. In the assessment year 1952 53 for which the account books were produced by the assessee, it claimed that the sums in question were not loans made in the ordinary course of its money lending business but were loans made out of funds lent by the Bombay firm as well as the moneys borrowed from the Bombay company. The Tribunal held that the amounts were not debts due to the assessee and that the assessee had no money lending interest or any other property. On appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The finding of fact is binding on the High Court and the Supreme Court. [ 423 C ] (2) It is true that the findings are conclusions of fact and those findings can be supported by evidence on record. But all the t ame it cannot be denied that the finding with regard to some other business of the assessee has come to certain ab rupt conclusions. [ 424 D E ] (3) The facts found by the tribunal are findings of fact. They clearly establish that the monies sent by the appellant to the Bombay firms were not loan ed in the normal course of their money lending or for any other business. [ 425 F G ] (4) The Tribunal has rightly pointed out that the statements of the witnesses examined by the Department were not sufficient to prove that the moneys sent by them to the Company were not the loans made by the company in the usual course of the business of its own. [ 426 B ] (5) The conclusion reached by the Tribunal is correct.

The petitioners in Special Leave Petitions were the owners of a piece of land situated at No. 11 A, L oni Road, Bangalore. They had constructed several buildings on the said lands. In respect of some other lands, they filed petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before this Court challenging the acquisition proceedings and also sought for a direction to the respondents to pay compensation as per the market value of the lands acquired. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners had not approached this Court with clean hands and therefore, there was no question of their being prevented from invoking the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 136 of the constitution. Hence these special leave petitions. Allow ing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners have come up with a case that the award made by the Land Acquisition Officer is without disclosing any facts. If he fails to do so and sup press es material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [ 588 C D ] 2. It is well settled that relief under Article 14 of the Land Acqu it tal cannot be granted unless there are compelling reasons to do not exist. [ 589 B ] 3. The Division Bench of the High Court has rightly held that the order of stay passed by this Court on September 20, 1984 would amount to suppression of material facts. [ 590 E F ] 4. The fact that the awards were not made within two years from the date of publication of the declaration under Section 4 of the Act does not attract the applicability of the principle of waiver. [ 591 G ] 5. The petitioner's claim that the acquisition was made beyond two years of the notification making the declaration must fail because the delay in filing the writ petition was only after three months. [ 592 H; 593 A ] 6. The writ petitions are allowed.

The appellant bank was a banking company. It had been carrying on business in the State of Mysore and its branches at different places. In the year 1959, it entered into an agreement with the Bank for granting to its employees who were drawing basic pay Rs. 175 as on January 1, 1959. On April 1, 1962, the appellant bank gave its staff scales to the respondent workmen. The respondent's claim that they should be given higher scale of pay was rejected by the Labour Court but the High Court allowed the application under Art. 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the award was not one of dismissal but of termination simpliciter and directed payment of full salary to the workman. Allow ing C. A. 1009 / 91, this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have taken the view that the words " shall be entitled to all increments provided in cl. (ii) of para 5 of the Sas try Award " mean that the actual pay of the employee is to be fixed at Rs. 190. [ 1009 B ] (ii). The word " shall " in clause (iv) means " shall ". This clearly indicates that the intention of the legislature was that the expression " shall ", used in cl s. (i), (ii), (iii) and (v) must be read together. If the meaning of the words are clear and unambiguous, then the court would give effect to the natural meaning of these words if there is any ambiguity or inconsistency between them and the context in which they occur. [ 1010 E F ] (iii)( a) The words " including " occurring in cl.( i) of the first part of cl. 2 (iv), namely, " shall also include " in the second part of the clause " shall mean " shall... " and " shall include " and the words'shall " and'shall'shall be construed accordingly; and (b) shall include anything done or omitted to be done before such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify in this behalf. [ 1011 D ] (iv)( a). The words'including'in cl (i)( ii) do not mean that it is only the final order passed by the Central Tribunal. The words are " shall, subject to the provisions of sub cl. 4, be exercised by the President and the Chairman." The words used in the first proviso are " may " and not " shall ";

The appellant, a registered society, was formed in the year 1958. It had been carrying on business of conducting hotels and lodging houses for its members. In the year 1968, it was decided to lease out the premises to the appellant's son ి who was also running a hotel. The lease deed provided that the lessee would pay rent at the rate of Rs. 300 per month for each room let out by him. The appellant paid the lease amount as well as the rent fixed under the lease. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit against the appellant for eviction of the appellant from the leased premises. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. On appeal, the High Court held that the lease was only for a period of 20 years and that the lessor i. e., the appellant could not be said to have created any rights or obligations in favour of the respondents. The High Court further held that there was no evidence to show that the appellants were ever put in possession of the leased property. The question whether the appellant had made an attempt to create a nuisance or to create nuisance is a mixed question of fact and law. The finding of the High court that the respondents were not entitled for any relief was set aside. The Division Bench allowed the appeal and directed the appellant to vacate the premises within six months. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts are right in their view that the lessees do not suffer any injury because they did not understand the difficulties which the owners of the properties would have faced if the lease were renewed. [ 280 B ] (2) The lease was for a particular period and the lessee was given the right to take the property on lease. If the lessee had committed any breach of the conditions of the lease, he could be evicted by taking recourse to the remedies available under the law. But the lessee cannot be compelled to make use of the property for the purpose of committing a nuisance. He can be evicted only after due process of law. [ 281 C D ] (3) The appellant has not shown that the other two mills were running the same industry. Therefore, the appellant cannot claim any relief against the respondents since the lease itself was for one year. [ 282 F ] (4) The order of the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court is set aside and the appellant is granted three weeks time to vacate.

The respondent assessee was a Hindu undivided family. On the death of one of his sons, his son and grand son, the assessee became entitled to the entire amount of Rs. 1 lakh which had been paid by him as his share in the firm. In the assessment year 1957 58 for the assessment years 1957 58 to 1958 59, the Income Tax Officer treated the sum of Rs 1, 50, 000 as the gift income from the firm and included it in the total income of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the gift was not true because the donor had no free right to the gift and so there could be no valid gift. The Tribunal also found that the gifts were made with the consent of the done e and hence the gift did not bind the done es. The High Court on reference confirmed the order of the Tribunal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The gift is not binding upon the assessee unless it is proved that the donor intended to make a gift of movable property or money's worth out of the joint family property. [ 100 E ] (ii) The fact that the assessee had a good and valuable life saving account would not affect the validity of the gift. It is well settled that if the donor has a full and complete legal title to the gifted property, he cannot take advantage of the provisions of section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act. [ 101 G H; 102 A B ] (iii) The object of the provision is to prevent fraud and to save transactions between persons who are not related to each other. If the transaction is such that the parties have entered into a transaction of sale of immovable property, it will be difficult to hold that the transaction was not effected with the intention of making a gift. [ 103 D F ] (iv) The words " without consideration " in section 123 of the Indian Succession Act, 18 89, must be given their ordinary meaning. They must be construed according to the context in which they appear in the instrument. The word " consideration " means adequate consideration. There is nothing in the deed which indicates that the consideration for the transfer was inadequate. The gift was made only to meet the needs of the transferor and the transferee. Therefore, the gift is invalid. [ 104 C D ] (v) The expression " without any consideration " used in section 122 does not mean that the donation should be made with a view to benefit the donor. The transaction is not a ben ami transaction but a transaction relating to the transfer of movable properties. The donor is required to pay the value of the property at the time of transfer. The property is not sold to the purchaser. The price is not an essential part of the transaction. The payment of the value is not necessary for the purpose of transferring the property. The value of such property is irrelevant.

The appellant was appointed as a super intendent of the police in the State of Orissa. He was posted at Cuttack on October 1, 1964 and he was transferred to Cuttack from that place. On November 15, 1966, he was posted as Superintendent of Police, Cuttack District. In February 1965, he made an application for transfer of certain officers to Cuttack during the period between October 11, 1961 and March 31, 1967. The Government rejected his request for transfer on the ground that it was not possible to accommodate him in any post in the secret ari at. The High Court held that the order of posting was passed by the government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court and therefore there was no question of any conflict between the two decisions. It also held that since the Chief Minister had already directed the Chief Secretary to make over charge to another officer, the Chief justice of the State could not have done so. The appellant contended before this Court that the Chief Ministers'orders were illegal because they did not take into account the Chief minister s'directions. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Chief Minister is entrusted with the responsibility of making transfers under his administrative control. If there is no such direction, the executive cannot do anything which may be inconsistent with the mandate of the Constitution. [ 10 66 B ] (2) The power of the Chief Jus tices to appoint or dismiss judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts is vested in the Chief Secretaries of the States. There is nothing in the Constitution which prevents the Chief or the State from doing what it does not want. [ 67 C D ] (3) The High Courts are not constituted courts of civil judic ature. They are tribunals set up to discharge quasi judicial functions. These tribunals are created by the Constitution Act. They function in their own fields. The powers of these bodies are co extensive with those of courts of law. The legislature can never enlarge them. But when they exercise their jurisdiction in respect of matters within their competence, they must be subject to the limitations prescribed by article 145 (1). [ 67 E F;

The appellant purchased the land in question from his co sharers. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for pre emption on the ground that he was not an agriculturist and did not hold any land in excess of the ceiling limit prescribed under section 15 (1)( b) of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale deed executed by the appellant in favour of the respondent No, 1 was hit by section 15 of the Punjab Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act, 1956 as it was not made after the coming into force of the said Act. On appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the appellant had failed to prove that the land sold by him was not in excess than what was prescribed under clause fourth ly of section 15. In further appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. It is well settled that if there is no ambiguity in the language used in clauses fourth ly or other sub sections of section 15th, the construction placed on the words " other co sharers " in clause fourth must be avoided. [ 128 C ] 2. The word'other'in clause'fourth ly means " such as " including ". This would mean that the legislature intended to exclude the word'others'from the scope of clause fourth. [ 129 D E ] 3. The expression'other co owners'in section 15 cannot be construed to include persons who are not included in the definition of'other '. The word " other'has been defined in section 2 (bb) of which the word " includes " is found in section 14 (1) (b).

The alien ees filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. They claimed that they were entitled to half share in the property as per their shares, but the trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no agreement between them and the alien ees regarding the sale deeds. On appeal by the alien ee, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and held that the alien ations were valid and the trans fere es had no interest in the properties which could be sold except on payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Ses hi ah and allowed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the High Courts order is erroneous because the alienation made by the purchasers was not binding on the alien ers and the purchaser cannot claim any right over the property unless the same has been duly registered. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that the alienation was void able. [ 543 D ] (2) The alienation was not vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation. It was not necessary that the parties should have entered into an agreement to sell the property. If the sale deed was executed without authority of law, the alien es would have no interest whatsoever in the said property. [ 544 G H; 545 A B ] (3) The alien ee can only get his name mutated in respect of the land under consideration and he can also execute a conveyance in favour of the alien er if he is willing to do so. But where the title is not clear, the transferee can always seek relief from the Civil Court. [ 546 F ] (4) The principle underlying section 16 (1)( b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is applicable to the facts of the case. [ 547 C ] (5) The doctrine of lis pend ens does not apply to the present case since the alien ants are not parties to the compromise nor are the alien ors who are parties to it. [ 548 E ] (6) The principles governing the grant of a decree or direction to a party to a suit are well settled. [ 549 E ] Per Subba Rao J. (concur ring): 1. The doctrine against assignment's of proprietary rights is inapplicable to the instant case inasmuch as the subject matter of the suit is not capable of being put to any particular use. [ 550 B ] 2. The principle behind Section 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that the Court must record a finding that there is a valid and lawful transfer of immovable property. This rule is based upon justice and equity. [ 551 B ] 3. The Court may appoint a Commissioner and take police help for executing this order and such cost shall ultimately be borne by the defaulting alien ees.

The appellants were employed by the respondent company in Baroda. They had been sick leave for a period of three months from July 1, 1975 to August 30, 1975 and they applied for the same on September 29, 1975. On June 8, 1975, the appellant company refused to grant the sick leave as it was not granted under the scheme of the Employees'State Insurance Act, 1948. The workmen filed an application before the Tribunal claiming that the sick ness benefit should be allowed to them with effect from December 14, 1969, but the Tribunal rejected their claim. The Company contended that the benefits admissible to the workmen under the Act could not be denied to them because of the failure of the Company to pay the employees'demand for sickness benefit. The Tribunal held that the benefit of the sick certificate would be available only if the sick industrial company has made out a case for sickness leave and that the workmen are entitled to such benefit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The sick leave is a pre condition for availing the sick or sick leave. It is a requirement which must be satisfied before the sick employee can avail of the sickness benefit; and that it cannot be said that the sickness leave is not a pre requisite for the purpose of the scheme. [ 86 C ] (ii) The Tribunal committed an error in holding that the appellant did not satisfy the requirements of section 49 of the Act. The provisions of the statute have to be construed strictly. [ 88 E F ] (iii) The words " no longer required " in section 49 (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act mean that the old provision does not apply to sick leave with retr o spe ctive effect. [ 89 D ] (iv) The expression " sick leave " in the context means " immediately preceding the date of sickness ". The word " immediately " in sub clause (b) of section 46 of the Factories Act means " reasonably practicable " and not " practicable " or " not practicable " in order to continue to do so in future.

The appellant, a detenu under detention in the State of Bombay was detained by an order made against him on June 8, 1955. He filed a petition before the High Court challenging his detention and the grounds of detention. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations were vague and that there was no material to support them. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the detaining authority had not stated any facts which would have influenced the mind of the detaining officer while making the order of detention; (2) that the detaining authorities did not consider the question as to whether or not the statements made by the detenue could be relied upon to sustain the order; and (3) that even if the allegations made in the grounds are assumed to be correct, they do not disclose any facts prejudicial to public interest. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22 (6) inasmuch as the obligation to furnish particulars is imposed only when the grounds must be disclosed. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) It is well settled that where the power is conferred upon the detaining Authority to furnish details of the grounds on which the satisfaction can be based, it cannot be said that the authority has not applied its mind to the relevant facts. If the detaining body has not given all the particulars, then the subjective satisfaction of the authority concerned cannot be questioned. But the fact that the grounds were supplied to the detenu does not mean that the Detaining Authority had not considered those facts. [ 32 G H ] (iii) The ground that the petitioner's representation was rejected without giving any particulars is bad because the detaining order itself states what the grounds actually refer ed to. [ 33 C D ] (iv) The contention that the ground taken in the affidavit in reply to the writ petition should be read as furnishing particulars is also ill founded. The fact that some of the averments made in para 15 (g) are contained in the counter affidavit of the Deputy Secretary shows that the Government has not been able to give any particulars at all. This is clear from the fact, that the respondent's case was that the documents referred to in paragraph 12 of the affidavit were not furnished.

The respondent was a commissioned officer. He was tried by the General Court Mar tial for an offence under section 19 of the, and the sentence was confirmed on appeal by the Chief Court mar tial. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, is ultra vires the. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Rule 14 of Army Rules 1954, provides that where a person subject to the Act is charged with an offence, he shall be liable to be cas hier ed or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. [ 10 75 C ] (2) Rule 15 of the Rules framed under the Act does not provide for removal of a person from service.

The appellant company was assessed to octroi duty in respect of certain goods. The assessment order was passed by the Panchayat on January 14, 1964. The Company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy and collection of octroi duty. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the resolution dated April 6, 1963, which authorised the levy of octroi had been validly made under r. 3 (b) of the Rules framed under the Act and ి the case of the Company. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (1) that the Resolution dated April 24, 1963 did not authorise the levy or collection of any octroi; (2) the resolution of the Panchayat approving the levy was invalid as it was beyond the powers conferred by r. 5 of the Taxation Rules; (3) the Resolution's fixing rates were ultra vires because they were not mentioned in the resolution; (4) the resolutions were invalid as they were contrary to the provisions of the Act; and (5) the imposition of octroi was illegal. HELD: (i) Rule 21 of the Bombay Excise (Oct roi) Rules, 1962 is valid and does not contraven e Art. 31 (1). [ 222 D ] (ii) The resolution dated February 25, 1963 was not invalid as being without authority of law. It was not necessary to specify the rate at which the tax could be imposed. The resolution merely stated that the Government would consider the proposal for imposing octroi duty within the limits of the Municipality. The Resolution was passed after considering all the relevant facts and circumstances. The question whether the resolution was valid or not did not arise. [ 223 F G ] (iii) The High court was right in holding that there was no proper publication of the notice under r 22. There was nothing in the rules to indicate that the procedure prescribed therein was followed. The rule making authority was entitled to do so.

The appellants were employed as workmen of the respondent company. They had been dismissed by the Company in December, 1951 on account of a strike which was illegal and void under section 31 (1) read with section 33 of the Act. On January 17, 1952, the Conciliation Officer made an order terminating the services of the appellants. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of dismissal on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction and that the conciliation proceedings should be deemed to have ended when the report was received by the appropriate Government. The High Court held that the Conciliation officer did not make his report within 14 days but only terminated the conciliation proceeding after expiry of 14 days from the date of receipt of the notice. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The conciliation proceedings must be deemed not to have commenced if no settlement is arrived at. If the conciliation officer does not make the report within the period specified in section 20 (2)( b), he cannot be said to have concluded the proceedings. [ 10 42 E ] (ii) Section 12 contemplates the submission of the report by the Conciliation Officers within 14 or 15 days. It is not necessary that the report should be made within 14 months. The conciliation officer may thereafter pass an order dismissing the workman concerned. But the question whether the conciliation Proceedings should be continued beyond 14 days or not depends upon how soon the report is received by him.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the, and he was arrested on November 3, 1985. He was taken into custody in connection with a case registered against him by the police authorities for offences under sections 147 / 149, 323 / 324 I. P. C. and section 27 (1)( d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989. The grounds of detention were served upon the detenu on December 14, 1985 and the order of detention was passed on January 6, 1986. The detaining authority after considering all the relevant factors including the allegations made against the detenu, passed an order of preventive detention against the petitioner on February 11, 1986, which was challenged before the High Court in Criminal Writ Petition No. 215 of 1986. A Single Judge of the High court quashed the order on the ground that there was no cogent material to justify the satisfaction of the detaining authority as contemplated by section 3 (2). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the order is bad because it did not indicate whether the detaining Authority had applied his mind to the facts mentioned therein; (ii) the detaining authorities have not considered the fact that the detenu was in jail and could not be released on bail; (iii) the orders of detention are vitiated because they were passed without application of mind and therefore the order was invalid; and (iv) since the order has been passed without applying its mind properly, the order suffers from non application of the mind. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The order of the detention is bad in law inasmuch as it does not state what consideration was given to the vital considerations or the circumstances mentioned in the said order. [ 10 42 B ] (2)( i) It is well settled that where the order affects the liberty of a person, the proper course is to pass such order. But if the order results in deprivation of personal liberty, the Court may not examine the reasons given by the detaining officer while passing the order. If the order does not show any application of judicial mind, the court would certainly not interfere. [ 43 E F ] (iii)( a) Where the order relates to maintenance of public order, the question whether the order should be revised or not must necessarily depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 44 G H ] (b) The power conferred on the appropriate Government under section 3 of the Act is very wide and can be exercised only when the order requires reconsideration. The order cannot be quashed merely on the basis of the statement of the District Magistrate who made it. [ 45 D ] (c) The expression " at the time of serving the order " occurring in section 3 4 (1), means that the order must be communicated to the detenu within five days of the making of the order, but it has to be communicated within seven days. The words " at least " make it clear that the detaining order must specify the period within which the representation shall be submitted. The word'forthwith'indicates that the action must be done within 48 Decision and Holding: (4) that the decision to detain is to be taken by the concerned authority within 60 days from the date of communication of the grounds of the Order to the detenue.

The appellant, a registered dealer under the provisions of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947, was carrying on business as a dealer in gold and silver ornaments. He filed his return for the assessment year 1959 57 showing the turnover of Rs. 6, 07, 000 / which included inter alia purchase price of gold ornaments weighing about 8, 14, 000 gms. The assessing authority held that the appellant had not furnished any data to show that he had purchased gold ornaments worth more than what he had acquired from the dealers and that the explanation offered by him was not convincing. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority but allowed the appeal holding that the restriction imposed by sec. 27 (6) was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not provide any objective standard or norm for the dealer to have regard to the number of dealers who were engaged in gold trade. In further appeal the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the assessing officer. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression'anticipated demand'has been used in some of the clauses under section 28. [ 10 B C ] 2. The word'anticipated'is capable of being construed liberally and its scope may be extended to include within it various situations such as those enumerated therein. It is not possible to accept the contention that the expression'actual'den otes only an estimate of the nature of the commodity intended to be bought and sold. [ 11 E F ] 3. The object of the Act is to prevent circum ven tion of the other provisions of sections 28 and 29. [ 12 G H; 12 A ] 4. The words " without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power " in sec. 28 are wide enough to take in every case where exemption is granted or refused. If the exemption is conditional upon the exercise of the discretion conferred by the section, the condition specified in the proviso must be fulfilled.

The appellants were the trustees of a temple in which they had been appointed as trustees. In 1946, the suit was filed by respondents 1 to 3 for possession of certain properties and for an injunction restraining the appellants from interfering with their possession. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the alien or had been removed from the management of the temple without his consent and that he had no right to interfere with the possession of the property. On appeal, the High Court held that the alienation made by the appellants was not bona fide and that it was not proved that the appellants had any title to the property and so, the decree passed by the lower appellate court was set aside. It further held that there was nothing to show that the plaintiffs had acquired title to this property by adverse possession. Held, that the finding of the trial judge that the transfer was not true could not be sustained. The fact that the manager of the trust had been transferred did not make him a trustee of the deity. The manager who was in charge of the management was merely managing the affairs of the institution and the manager cannot be said to have acted as de facto man agers of the endowment. The appellants'case that the suit should have been dismissed under article 134 B of the Limitation Act must fail. Per Sarkar and H id ayat ullah, JJ. (i) The appellants had been rightly found to have acquired title by adverse Possession against the respondent No. 4. The High Court was wrong in holding that the sale deed executed by the manager in favour of the appellants'predecessor was invalid. (ii) That the appellants were entitled to recover possession of all the properties and the suit lands having been purchased by them by means of a registered sale deed, the appellants could not claim any benefit under section 43 of the Specific Relief Act. (iii) The High court was wrong when it held that even if the appellants failed to establish that the original owner was in possession of some of the properties, the same would not amount to adverse possession within the meaning of section 43 Of the Indian E ase ment Act.

The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on the business of cinema at Sim la in the State of Jammu and Kashmir filed an application under section 3 (1) of the Jammu & Kashmir Cin em as (Regulation) Act, 1972 for grant of a licence to run a Cinema Theatre. The District Magistrate granted the said licence subject to certain conditions mentioned therein. The appellant challenged the validity of the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of the Act and the Rules were not applicable to the cinema theatre inasmuch as they did not have any statutory right other than those contained in the Act or the Rules and therefore the impugned order was bad in law. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 3 (3) of The Cin emato graph Act, 1952 are intended to regulate exhibition of cin emato graph films in the cinema hall's where public exhibition is permitted by the licensing authority. [ 594 F ] 2. The expression " any other person " occurring in sub section (3)( b) of section 3 of the Cin emato graphic Act, 1955 must be given its natural meaning and no artificial ity can be attributed to the provision. It cannot be construed to mean that the licensee has no power to grant licences in respect of the theatre. If the intention of the legislature was to permit exhibition of films in cinema theatre without a licence there would have been no necessity to use the words " such licence ". But if the intention was to conduct the exhibition of film in the'Theatre ', then the word " exhibition " could only mean exhibition of the cin emato graphic film with the object of making it available for exhibition. [ 595 C D ] 3. The word " licence " used in section 3 is clear and unambiguous and does not mean that every licence granted in favour of the licensee must always be for the purpose of undertaking exhibition of cinema. [ 596 B ] 4. The words " any licence or permission " in section 2 (d) of Act means a licence granted for the manufacture of cin em as and not a licence for the purposes of the Public exhibition of a cin emato graphy apparatus. The definition of " licence ", as given in section 5 (c) of that Act, shows that what is done by the licensee is to conduct his business in a cinema theatre with a licence in respect thereof. The licence granted to the respondent was a licence issued for running a cinema theater with a building. The cinema theatre is a cinema house. The terms and conditions of the licence show that the licence is for running the cinema theater and not of cinema theatre. The fact that the cinema shows are less than one fourth of the total number of seats in the building of the cinema premises makes no difference because the licence covers the cinema the cinema itself. [ 597 H;

The appellants, who were the owners of a mill and had been allotted to them by the Custodian under the provisions of the, on December 2, 1954, applied for allotment of the mills in their favour. They also applied for the issue of a notification under section 12 (1) of the Dis placed Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 (44 of 1954), declaring that they were entitled to be put in possession of the said mills and factory properties as evacuee property. The respondent contended that the notices issued by the competent authorities under the Act did not amount to an acquisition of rights within the meaning of article 31 (2) of Constitution and therefore the notice was invalid. Held, that the notice dated September 5, 1955, was valid and it could not be challenged in view of the provisions contained in section 10 of the Act which provides that no person shall be entitled to any compensation or other benefit under any law for the time being in force unless he has been given an opportunity of being heard.

The appellant was a minor son of the deceased. He filed an application under section 21 (1) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Res um ption of Jagir's Act, 1955 for consolidation of his land in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 1955. The Sub Divisional Officer passed an order on 6th August, 1972 holding that the ceiling area had been determined according to old law i. e. Act of 1973 and it was not open to him to question any decree or orders passed by the Sub Divisional officer in exercise of his powers under Section 221 of the. Act. On appeal, the Additional District Judge set aside the order of the Sub divisional Officer and remanded the case to the Sub Judge for fresh disposal after giving opportunity to both sides to adduce evidence. The High Court held that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside its earlier order dated 5th May, 1976 and directed the Sub division officer to dispose of the appeal afresh. In the appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (1). Under section 223 of the Government of India Act of 1935, the power of the Board to make rules relating to matters provided for in Chapter III B of the Constitution was only limited to the executive powers of the State; (2) Rule 13 A of the Rules framed under the Act Of 1955 did not empower the Board of Revenue to set up additional revenue courts in respect of matters which were pending at the time when the new Act came into force. (3) Rule 14 of the Central Provinces and Ber ar Regulation of Agricultural Le ases Act, 1949, does not confer any power on the Board so as to bring it within the purview of the said rule. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The power conferred on the board is vested in the Board under section 222 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 18 79. [ 10 31 C ] (ii) The Board has power to set apart land for agricultural purposes and vest it in another body. It cannot be said that there is no provision for separate unit in Chapter II B of 1948. The power of superintendence given to the Board is different from the power to interfere with the judicial proceedings. [ 11 E F ] (iii) The scheme of the Land Revenue Act, 18 53, indicates that the legislature intended to deal with the functions of the Revenue Courts and the powers of such officers are vested in them. The Legislature could not have intended to create a new head of administration without express provision in the Act. But if the subordinate court dis charges its duty of framing the issues affecting the rights of parties, it would be difficult to hold that the power exercised by the Board was not subject to the same rules applicable to the superior courts.

The appellant, a newspaper establishment of the State of Maharashtra was carrying on business in news and paper. It had been publishing daily newspapers from time to time as also by other newspapers. In the course of its business it published news reports for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the publication of the said law reports, it would be difficult to have one opinion on the question whether the publication should be restricted to one or more than one newspaper. The appellant's case was that the publication was not confined only to one newspaper but to several other newspapers which were published in different langu ages. The High Court held that the expression " newspaper " used in section 2 (b) of the Act included not merely newspapers but also newspapers and since the publication did not involve any publication of a newspaper, the provisions of the section were not attracted. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " public news " has been defined in section 3 (d) of, the Press and Registration of Books Act, 18 67, and the definition of " newspaper ", given in section 4 thereof, includes not merely " a matter of public history but also every piece of information relating to matters connected with the administration of the affairs of the country ". [ 565 C ] 2. The word " newspaper'is defined in the Act as a newspaper as including a periodical or periodical publication made by the Central Government or by a local authority. The term'newspaper'has been used in the dictionary meaning of the word'newspaper '. The dictionary meaning is " a medium of exchange of news, papers, books, periodical s, etc., e. g. a newspaper; an ency cl oped ia, a number of forms, letters, figures, etc. The dictionary gives the meaning of a particular expression in the context of the Indian Language Dictionary. The same dictionary defines the word " paper " as " a large volume of writing, a small part of a document, a series of words, a general description, a large number of words and a variety of meanings." The dictionary uses the word, " paper ", " printing " and " mag az ine " as a medium or large number. The use of the words " paper and paper " in the Shor ter Oxford English Dictionary, referred to above, shows that the meaning assigned to the word paper is " paper, a medium, a book, a paper, an article or a book or a paper or a record, a plan, plan, article, note, or a list of articles, or materials, either generally or in addition to some fixed objects, such as books, pam ph lets, paper boards, etc.; the word is normally understood as a whole, but it does not mean that all the items of the paper are meant for the use of a few people who may be interested in knowing the contents of the article or the language spoken therein. The test laid down by this Court in the aforesaid decision is that the words must be given their ordinary meaning.

The appellant was a licensee under the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947. He filed an application for leave to defend his possession on the ground that he had sub let the premises in question to one Shri N. D. Mani ar and others who were tenants of the appellant firm. On August 1, 1969 the appellant filed an eviction petition against respondent No. 2 alleging that he was a tenant of the premises which was leased by him to M / s. B right Br os. (P) Ltd., at a monthly rent of Rs. 40, 000. The said application was dismissed by the trial court holding that it was not a lease but a licence. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the agreement between the parties was a lease and not a licence, the provisions of section 5 (4A) would be applicable and the appellant could not be evicted from the premises unless he was put in possession of the same. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 5 (4) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act is a special law enacted by Parliament with respect to the control of rents and repairs and other matters connected therewith. It is well settled that the general law of tenancy laws relating to landlord and tenant is substantially similar to the Rent Acts in force in England. [ 10 69 C ] 2. The object underlying the statute is to protect the interests of the landlords as well as the tenants and to prevent exploitation of landlords'property by unscrupulous landlords. The legislature has taken care to see that the landlords are not allowed to explo it their own properties by creating third party rights or otherwise. This is so because the Legislature has chosen to make such a provision. The purpose of the Act is to provide protection to the tenants against exploitation by landlords who have no longer occupied the premises. If the intention of the Legislature was to protect only those persons who have been in occupation of the tenanted premises and not licensees, then there was no reason why the Legislature should have made a provision like section 5 A of the Delhi Rent Control and Eviction Act, 1958. [ 1072 F G; 1073 A B ] 3. The expression " statutory tenancy " in section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act means a contractual relationship between the landlord and the tenant and cannot be equated with a contractual tenancy. The word " statutory " is normally used in a very wide sense. But where the context requires something more than mere use, such as possession, the test is whether it is a contract of tenancy or a contract. There is nothing in the language of the section which suggests that the legislature intended to exclude cases where the tenancy is created by contract or by operation of law. [ 1073 H; 1073 E ] 4. The words " statutory tenant " in clause (3) of section 6 mean a person who holds land under a lease or leases the premises or any part thereof. The definition does not include a lessee or a sub tenant. [ 1074 B ] 5. The term " statutory lease " is defined in section 2 (bb) of The Bombay Rent Decision and Holding: Act, 1970. The meaning of the word " Statutory " is " a written agreement between a landlord and a tenant ". The definition of " statutory term " is inclusive of the period during which the tenant may remain in possession after the determination of the tenancy.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948 under a deed of partnership dated January 26, 1950. Under this deed it was agreed that the appellant would be entitled to refund of the amount paid by it for the period between August 15, 1947 and December 2, 1947 on account of the failure of certain conditions to pay the amount due from it. In accordance with the covenant contained in the agreement the appellant became liable to pay interest at 4 % per annum on the amounts which were outstanding as on April 1, 1949. On March 19, 1951, the Government of Rajasthan issued a notification under section 3 (1) of the United State of Rajasthan Act No. XX VI of 1947 declaring its intention to apply the United States of Rajasthan as it was then known as the " Rul er " of the former Indian State of Sir ohi. By another notification dated June 28, 1953, the United Provinces Government declared its intention of taking over all the territories of the State including Jaipur and the United Bharat Mills. The appellant claimed exemption from payment of sales tax on the ground that the merger took place before January 26. 1950 and therefore the liability to pay sales tax could not be enforced against it. Held, that the contention must fail. The question whether the appellant had any enforceable right to claim refund arose only after the Constitution came into force and the appellant was not bound by the provisions of article 295 (2) of India (Trans l ation by Ac ced ing to the Constitution) of Part B of the Constitution.

The appellants, a registered dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, were carrying on business in cotton and other commodities. They had been assessed to sales tax for the years 1954 - 55 and 1955 11 respectively on the footing that they were not dealers within the meaning of section 2 (d) of the Act. The assessment orders made by the assessing authority were confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but the High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression " commercial crops " occurring in section 5 (1) of Act 47 of 1953 would include " any transaction in respect of which no fee is payable by or on behalf of a trader ". Held: (i) that the word " commercial " in section 14 must be given its ordinary gram matical meaning so as to cover transactions which are not genuine ly entered into by traders with the object of ev ading the payment of tax; (ii) that if the legislature intended to exclude from the price or commodity charged by a seller who is not a trader, such a construction should be avoided; (iii) where a sale is effected by transfer of property in goods whether prior to or after the execution of a conveyance, delivery of possession thereof, then the sale will be deemed to have taken place inside the State of Tamil Nadu; (iv) that there is nothing in the language of section 14 to suggest that the words'for the purpose of the said section'mean only a resale of the goods sold and not the goods themselves; and (v) that even if the words " for the purposes of the aforesaid Act " were construed to mean " for use by the purchaser ", the intention could be gathered from the fact that the goods were actually delivered at the time of the execution thereof.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to this Court by special leave against his conviction, but that appeal was dismissed on the ground that there were no reasons for reducing the sentence. In the present case also, the High Court did not accept the contention that the conviction was bad because it had not been made in accordance with law. Held: (i) That the sentence of death is a matter of discretion and courts have always recognised that the discretion has to be exercised judicially. It is open to the court to impose such punishment as it thinks fit. But where the offence committed is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, then unless there are special reasons to justify the extreme penalty, the discretion cannot be invoked except when the sentence is so disproportionate to the gravity of the offence itself as to shock the conscience of the court. State of U. P. vs Em per or,;, referred to. (ii) There is nothing in the Evidence Act which shows that the presumption of innocence can be raised only if the prosecution has established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused has committed the offence.

The petitioners in the writ petition were working as Executive Engineers in the Public Works Department of the Government of India. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) and they were promoted on officiating basis to the said post with effect from 5. 11. 1976. On their promotion, the petitioner was reverted to his substantive post by an order dated 25. 5. 1954. He filed a Writ Petition No. 56 / 1973 before the High Court challenging the orders of compulsory retirement made against him. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners had not attained the age of 55 years at the time when they were compulsorily retired under Fundamental Rule 56 (j). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants: (1) that the impugned order of compulsory retire ment was passed without affording any opportunity of hearing to the petitioners; (2) that there was no provision in the Fundamental Rules which required the authorities to give notice to the public servant concerned before exercising power of compulsory Retirement; (3) that even if the impugned orders were held to be invalid, the same could not be sustained because the principles of natural justice were violated; (4) that since the impugned action is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution, the impugned notices are liable to be quashed; and (5) that in view of the fact that the petitioner has been retired after attaining the age 55 years, he would have become entitled to the benefit of the Fundamental Rule 51 A (j); and (6) that though the impugned proceedings were initiated by the respondents pursuant to the directions given by the Central Government, the petitioners did not exercise the right conferred by the Fundamental rules but exercised the power of premature retirement. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned orders of the Central Administrative Tribunal and the High court are set aside. [ 960 G ] 2. The petitioners who joined the service of the respondent department in the year 1975 and were promoted as officiating Executive Engineers, were in Class I or Class II service or post, whether substantively or on officiating, till the date of superannuation. The question whether the petitioners should be treated as having acquired the requisite qualification for being considered for the purpose of pension does not arise.

The appellant Corporation had taken a policy for the life insurance of its employees. On the death of one of its officers, the Life Insurance Corporation was informed that it would be accepting the proposal subject to certain conditions and in consideration of the payment of premium, the Corporation would accept the proposal. In the letter dated 23rd December, 1963 addressed by the Divisional Manager to the Executive Officer of the Corporation, the appellant company stated that the amount of premium payable under the policies would be accepted only after the receipt of the proposal from the Corporation and not thereafter. The appellant corporation however did not receive any response to the said letter. Thereafter, on 11th January, 1961, the Executive Engineer wrote to the Divisional Office requesting the appellant Corporation to reconsider the matter and to pay back the sum assured with interest at six per cent per annum. The Divisional Manager replied on 12th February, 1964 stating that the proposal could not be accepted as he had already accepted the proposal but he had declined to accept the same. The Corporation then issued a notice calling upon the appellant to pay the entire sum assured together with interest within 15 days. The respondent filed a suit challenging the validity of the notice contending inter alia that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation; that the claim was barred by limitation; that even if the proposal was accepted, the amount paid was not liable to be forfeited; that since the proposal had been accepted, there was a concluded contract of insurance; and that the repudiation of the claim made by the Corporation was illegal; and further contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that there were no concluded contracts.
