The trial court dismissed the suit. The first appellate court confirmed the decree of the trial court. The High Court affirmed the decision of the courts below. Dismis sing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The expression " under writing " is used in Chapter III of the Financial Powers of the Standing Order. It is clear that once an acceptance is communicated to the offer or, where the proposal is received before the time specified in the communication, the acceptance must be communicated to him. [ 361 B ] 2. The word'accept'has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary (6th Edition) at page 12 71 thus: " Where, therefore, the person who accepts the proposal agrees to accept it without anything more, the agreement may be regarded as an acceptance; but so far as the acceptance is concerned, the act of acceptance may be expressed in such circumstances as to make it known that the acceptance was intended to take effect immediately." The mere fact that the draft was prepared and approved does not mean that the contract was not complete until the date of acceptance was communicated to it. The words " under stands " are very significant. They indicate that the intention of the parties was to accept what they actually do and not merely to accept something which might have been done. The intention is to be gathered from the terms of the contract itself. If the contract is not complete till the date fixed, the question of acceptance will not arise. [ 362 C D ] 3. The term " under Decision and Holding: " is wide enough to include acceptance of the proposals. [ 363 F ] 4. The object of the Act is to prevent fraud and to provide for speedy remedy to the victims of accidents arising out of accidents caused by use of motor vehicles. The provisions of section 80 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, clearly show that the legislature intended to give effect to the legislative intent contained in the said section. [ 366 A B ] 5.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the order of the High Court refusing to grant an interim injunction was illegal and void. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the order granting the certificate did not determine any rights or obligations of the parties in dispute in the suit. On appeal, the High court held that the decision of the Federal Court was final and conclusive and therefore there could be no question of the plaintiff being entitled to obtain a decree for possession of the property in dispute. In appeal by special leave, Held: (1) that the High Courts have power under article 133 (1)( a) to issue writs for quashing orders passed by the courts subordinate to them in exercise of their powers under section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, to pass such orders as they think fit with respect to matters in controversy between the parties. (2) that where the High'Court has refused to exercise its discretion under article 226 of the Constitution, it cannot interfere with the discretion exercised by the High. Court because it is concerned only with the determination of the right or obligation of the party against whom the writ is sought.

The appellant company was manufacturing cloth and the process or's expenses were incidental to the sale of processed fabric. The appellant, a manufacturer of fabrics, had sold the processed fabric in the market as it was then manufactured by another person who was also selling the same goods. The excise authorities held that the assessable value of the processed fabrics should be taken into consideration for determining the assessable Value of the grey cloth plus the cost of job work done plus profit and the manufacturing expenses. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant is not a manufacturer but only a trader. It is necessary to include the process ors, costs and charges plus profit. [ 173 C ] (2) The fact that the appellant has been manufacturing cloth from one person to another would make no difference since the process carried out by the two persons are different and distinct. [ 174 B ] (3) In order to determine whether the assessable values have been correctly arrived at, the proper officer must take into account all relevant facts including the processes or'expenses incurred and labour charges plus profits and the sales tax paid thereon.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 13, 1973. He was promoted to the post of Head Clerk in January 1974 and he continued to work there till April 1, 1975 when he was absorbed in Government service. On April 1. 1975, he was appointed temporarily as a peon in the Panchayat Samiti. In February 1975, the appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk. The appellant filed an application before the High Court for a direction that his services be regularised with effect from April 1 1975. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that since the appointment of the appellant as a head clerk was not made by way of promotion within the meaning of clause (b) of section 14 (4) of the Amending Act, it had no power to make appointments to the posts of a Head Clerks under the proviso to sub section (3) of Section 15 of the Act. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of a person to the Post of a head Clerk is not a permanent one and therefore, cannot be equated with a permanent employee. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The term'permanent'has been defined in Explanation II to section 14 of the Rajasthan Panchayat Act, 1953 which defines " permanent servant ". It means any person who holds substantively a permanent or temporary post. A person holding a post in a substantive capacity in a temporary capacity would be considered to be a permanent member if he is permanently appointed to that post. If the appointment is made without the authority of law, it would be deemed to have been made after the date of such appointment. [ 1032 F G ] 3. The word'permanent ', in the context, must be given its ordinary meaning. There can be no doubt that the expression'permanent post'in the proviso is wide enough to include all kinds of posts including those of a ministerial staff.

The appellant Mahant Shiv sh ankar Y ati was the f ounder of a religious institution known as Sri Thakur ji's Math. He died in 19 17 leaving behind his widow and two sons, namely, the respondent and one daughter who was married to the deity. In 1922, the property devol ved on her son, the father of the respondent, who was then minor at that time. On his death, the appellant filed an application under section 5 (1) of the U. P. Act No. XXX IX of 1949 for exemption from the levy of tax on the income of the properties belonging to the Math and the deity, contending that the properties were not the personal properties of the Mahant but belonged to him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the property was the personal property of the Math, and held that it was the property of Shri Thakur which was acquired by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High court has rightly rejected the claim of the appellant that the amount of Rs. 45, 000 was paid to the respondent as his personal income.

The appellants were allotted certain lands in the village Rai kot. They had been allotted some of these lands by the Custodian, but they did not take possession thereof and so their allotment was cancelled under section 12 (1) of the Act. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the cancellation of allotment on various grounds. It was contended that there was no provision for cancellation of allotments made by the Deputy Custodian General or the Custodian ి an officer appointed under the Act to cancel an allotment. Held: (i) The provisions of section 10 of the Administration of E vac uee Property Act, 1950, which provide for cancellation or suspension of allotment are contained in sections 12 and 19 of the 1954 Act. Section 11 of the said Act provides that where any property is declared to be evacuee property under section 13, the Custodian shall make an order declaring such property to be forfeited to the State Government as being evacuee property. Under section 12, if the property has been acquired by the Central Government under the provisions of the E vac ue es (Administration of Property) Act, 1951, it would be deemed to have vested in the Custodian with all the powers of management and control of the evacuee properties. The only other thing which can be done under section 11 is that the property should be restored to the person from whom it was acquired. If the property is restored to him he will be entitled to get back the money paid over. He cannot claim refund of the amount paid by him because the Custodian does not retain the property.

The appellants were selected for the post of Upper Division Clerk in the Public Service Commission. They challenged the selection on various grounds, inter alia, that they had been deprived of their right to be considered for appointment as Lower Division Clerks and that the process of re g aining experience was illegal. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that there was no justification for cancellation of the recruitment examination and directed the State Government to re do the same. In appeal by special leave it was contended before this Court: (1) that the advertisement did not provide for re g ard ing or re considering the written examination but only provided a fresh interview; (2) that if the candidates who had earlier appeared at the written test had failed to get themselves interviewed, then the entire recruitment would have to be cancelled; (3) that since the original examination was over and the results were yet to be declared, the subsequent re g istr ation could not have been cancelled; and (4) that even though the original examin a tion was over, the second re g ister ed examination was held after the result was declared. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The High Courts order is unsustainable. [ 173 E ] (ii) There has been no proper re g ulation of the facts alleged. The conduct of the appellant itself shows that he was trying to get down from the competitive examination. He had also tried to sc utt le the recruitment process. It was not his case that he had been denied any opportunity to cross examine the witnesses. [ 174 B C ] (iii) The fact that the original exam was over does not mean that the fresh interview was done.

The appellant, a member of the D era and its properties, filed a suit against the respondent for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that he was not a necessary party to the suit as he had no interest in the property of the respondent. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to be impleaded as a party under Order 22, rule 10 because he was elected to the D ara and the properties appertaining to it were the subject matter of the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court erred in allowing the appeal and setting aside the decree of the trial court. [ 384 C ] (2) A person who is elected to fill his place does not become a party to an action or suit merely because at the time when he becomes a ma h ant of the institution of the cause of action he dies. He cannot be added as a person either as a plaintiff or as a de facto ma h ants unless there is some change in his mind. [ 385 B ] (3) The principle underlying section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that where a person succeeds to the estate of another he can be added in order to bring about the same result. If the case falls within the provisions of Order 22 Rule 10, the former has to be substituted as a proper party under the said provision. It is only when a person succeeded to the property belonging to another person that he would be a necessary or proper party to enable him to be added. But if the person succeeding is not a proper person, then the transferee should be made a necessary one to represent the interests of the other party. [ 386 F G ] (4) The expression " legal representative " used in O. 22, r. 10 means a person who represents himself as such but whose interest is adverse to the party claiming it. [ 387 E ] (5) The word'deceased'occurring in O X R 22, R. 10 includes a person representing the deceased party. The words'legal representative'are wide enough to include a person nominated by the party to be joined as a legal representative of the deceased. The word " legal " indicates that the person who represented the estate must be the real heir of the estate. [ 388 H; 389 A ] (6) The right of the successor to sue survives after the death of the defendant. The interest of the person in the subject matters of the claim lies in the person claiming it and not in the representative capacity.

The petitioners, who were working as Sub Inspectors of Police in the Andhra Pradesh State Police Service, challenged the validity of the Rules and amendments made to the Fundamental Rules by which they were conferred with a vested right to be considered for promotion to the higher post of Inspector. They also challenged the amendment made to their Fundamental Rules on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as it violated Article 311 (2) of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the impugned amendments were not violative of the provisions of the Fundamental rules but only the executive instructions issued under the proviso to Article 309 of the Con stitution. Dismis sing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The power to amend the Fundamental Rule is conferred by the Legislature itself. It cannot be said that the exercise of the power conferred by Article 309 is arbitrary or unreasonable. [ 590 C ] 2. The amending power conferred under the Proviso to Article 3 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution is an independent power and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily. It is not open to the Courts to substitute its own views for those of the legislature. [ 591 F G ] 3. The amended Fundamental Rules are not ultra vires the Constitution nor can they be amended retrospectively so as to violate the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the'Constitution. [ 592 B ] 4. In view of the fact that the power to legislate has been delegated to the Legislature by the Governor, the Legislature cannot be accused of having passed a law for an extraneous purpose. [ 589 D ] 5. The object of the amendment introduced by the Amending Act is to give effect to the directive principles contained in article 39 (b) and to make the equality of citizens available to all persons within the territory of India. [ 593 A B ] 6. The amendment made by the impugned amendment introducing the new rule 2 (10) in the Fundamental'Rules is invalid because it violates Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. The impugned amendment is valid.

The appellants are manufacturers of various kinds of goods falling under section 9 (1) and the raw materials purchased by them from their principal s. They filed returns for the assessment years in question, claiming that they were not liable to tax on the purchases made by them but were liable to pay tax under section 6 of the C. S. T. Act, 1948. The assessing authority held that the purchase turnover was liable to be assessed as a purchase tax under the provisions of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority. In further appeals, the Tribunal held that since the purchases had been made by the assessees themselves, it could not be said that the purchases were liable or taxable at the point of time when the goods were actually sold. The High Court dismissed the petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The purchases effected by the appellants were not exempt from tax under Section 6 of C. T., 1956. [ 11 B ] 2. The purchase of raw materials by the assessee is also liable to the tax under sections 9 and 24 (3). [ 11 D ] 3. The sales of manufactured goods which attract the provisions contained in section 6 must be deemed to have taken place within the meaning of section 5 (1)( b) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The sale of such goods would be liable to State Sales Tax only if the goods are actually sold or otherwise disposed of. [ 12 E F ] 4. The contention of the assessees that the sales of goods made by dealers who do not fall under section 2 (p) read with section 15 of the Bombay Sales Tax, Act, 19 01 cannot be taxed at the rate applicable to them because the sales in the present case are not exempted under section 5 of the CST Act.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to purchase tax under section 10 (b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The assessment order was made on September 30, 1956. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the assessment and the appellate authority confirmed the assessment. The High Court held that the sales were exempted from tax under article 286 (1)( b) as they were not sales in the course of export within the meaning of section 5 (2). In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the words " a person " in section 10 are wide enough to include a registered assessee who has sold goods to him or any other person. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The word " a " is normally dis jun ctive ly used in every taxing statute. It is not possible to hold that when the goods have been despatched outside the State of Bombay, the sale must be deemed to have taken place inside the State if the goods are actually carried out. [ 11 B ] (ii) The expression " a registered person " is wide enough not only to den ote such a person but also to include the immediate importer or consignee. If the intention is to carry out the import of goods then the sale would be exempt from tax. Therefore, the words'a person'in section 8 (b), namely, the seller will have to be construed as having the same meaning as given in section 6 of the Central Sales Tax, Act. [ 12 G H; 13 A C ] (iii) The words " at the time of shipment " do not mean that the goods should be actually ship ped or ship ped. They can be imported into India either by a registered importer or by a person who is not a registered. The words'at the point of time of the shipment'cannot be interpreted to exclude a registered buyer from the purview of the words "' a person ".

The respondent husband was the wife of a second wife. He filed an application for maintenance under section 125 (3) (b) against her husband and his family members, who were minors at the time of divorce. The Magistrate held that the first payment by way of customary or personal law to the respondent was not in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the parties and therefore he had no jurisdiction to order the respondent to pay any amount as maintenance allowance. On appeal, the Sessions Judge set aside the order of the trial court and directed the respondent's husband to pay a sum of Rs. 5, 000 per month to the appellant from the date of the decree till the date on which she is entitled to maintenance. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the second payment by the respondent would not be in compliance with the direction given by the Magistrate to the wife to maintain herself but should have taken into account the fact that the respondent had been divorced by him during his life time and that the third payment made by him was towards the maintenance of the respondent. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The liability to provide maintenance does not depend upon the nature of the relationship between the spouses. It is only when the parties agree to live separately after mutual consent that the obligation to maintain the wife can be enforced. [ 10 31 B ] 2. A second payment may be made if the marriage has been ir retriev ably broken down because of the fear of the defendant or his agent or other person acting in collusion with the second party. But where the second one is not agreed upon, the second is not contemplated by section 127 (3)( b). The second payment is not necessarily covered by the second part of the section. [ 11 D E ] 3. Section 127 (4) provides that the payment of maintenance will be subject to the conditions mentioned therein. If the second proviso is read with section 127, it is clear that the condition precedent to the applicability of the second limb is that the maintenance must be paid out of the matrimonial home. This is what the legislature intended. [ 12 C F ] 4. The second proviso to section 127 is a social purpose, not a ben ign ant or sub tle. It cannot be construed to mean that the Legislature intended to grant relief to the second wife without ascertaining the actual state of affairs. [ 13 G H;

The appellant was a successful bidder in respect of the tender for the year 1988. He submitted his bid on 25. 3. 88 and he was called upon to submit his representation within 15 days from the date of issue of the order. On 26. 3 1988, the appellant made an application before the Collector stating that he had no objection to the black listing order dated 25. 03. 1988 passed by the Collector. The Collector rejected the same holding that there was no requirement in the rule of natural justice that any person should have been heard before black listing the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition challenging the order of the Collector as well as the Government's order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State Government that the order did not contain any notice or opportunity of making representations against the order and that the appellant was entitled to be heard before the black list was issued. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of black listing is set aside. [ 779 E ] 2. The question whether the appellant has a right to be considered for future contracts under the Collector is a matter which can be decided only after giving the parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his own use and occupation. The Rent Controller decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that: (i) section 10 (2)( vii) of the Act is not applicable as there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties; (ii) Section 11 (1) of Act does not apply to a case where the landlord has failed to prove the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in sub section (1); (iii) Section 10 (1)( c) provides that if the court is satisfied that the building is bona fide required by the landlord for the purpose of its business or for any other purpose for which it is reasonably expected to be let from the landlord, it shall pass an order directing the tenant to put the landlord into possession. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1). The expression " for the purposes of this Act " in section 4 (1), means only one of the two situations contemplated under section 4. It is not possible to lay down any inf lex ible rule that when the legislature uses the word'for'the first part of section 4, it will have to be given its ordinary meaning. [ 571 C ] (2) The words " for any reason whatsoever " are wide enough to include a situation where the rent is not paid by the tenant but is paid by him. If the landlord chooses to do so, he must be held to have done something which is in excess of the amount of rent actually payable by the tenants. This would be so even though the landlord may not be able to show that the tenant had committed some wrong act in respect of the property. [ 572 G H ] (3) The language of section 10 is very clear and unambiguous. There is nothing in the language of the section which makes it plain that the legislature intended to give a restricted meaning to the term " for such ". [ 573 F ] (4) The Legislature could not have intended to exclude cases where the tenancy was created before the coming into force of the Rent Control Act. But the legislature did not choose to make any distinction between cases where a landlord and a tenant were entitled to seek fixation of fair rent. [ 573 B D ] (5) The object of the legislature in enacting section 4 is to provide for a machinery for recovery of the dues of the landlord. The legislature has clearly provided for a remedy for recovery by the landlords. The landlord can recover the amount either by instituting a suit or proceeding against the tenant. The right of the landlords to recover the arrears of rent is expressly taken away. [ 574 E ] (6) The provisions of section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code are not exhaustive. They cannot control the provision contained in section 10. The power conferred on the Rent Controller by section 10 of the Madras City Ten ants'Protection Act, 1947 is not an un guided or arbitrary power.

The petitioner respondent was a permanent and non gazetted officer in the State of Mysore. He was appointed as an Assistant Engineer on probation for a period of two years, but he was reverted to his substantive post with effect from April 6, 1962. On the basis of certain complaints made by him against the petitioner, the Central Government referred the matter to the High Court under section 115 (5) of the Act. The High Court held that the petitioner had not been given any opportunity to make representations and that the Central Govern ment could not be compelled to give him fresh seniority list. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the principles laid down in the case of Prabha val kar's case (supra) would apply only if there is no element of mala fides or where the reasons are absent. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The principle underlying the provisions of the statute must be borne in mind when considering whether a particular decision can be said to be vitiated by non observance of the conditions pre ce p tible of being challenged. [ 10 56 G ] 2. The power of the courts to see that an authority has acted properly in accordance with the statute cannot be questioned merely because some mistakes have crept into the decision of the authorities concerned. If the court comes to the conclusion that the error committed by the authorities is such that it would be possible to set right the wrong, it may interfere even though the mistake might not have been committed. But the question is whether the courts should exercise their power of judicial review in respect of orders passed by them which are based on irrelevant considerations or upon extraneous considerations. [ 11 E F; 11 A B ] 3. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the High court under Article 226 of the Constitution is limited to seeing that an act done judicially in accordance therewith does not violate the law or is illegal or unjust. [ 12 C D ] 4. The writ petitions filed by the respondents challenging the final list prepared by the Central Govt. are without merit and they are liable to be dismissed.

The appellants, manufacturers of " Ro lled Jute Y arn " were selling the " Ro ller " and " Pr inter " to their customers. They sold the " Pr inted Ro lled Ro lled Clo sure " from the factory premises of the buyer on payment of a price of Rs. 5 per kg. by them in wholesale market at the factory gate. The price charged by the buyers for the " ro ller " was not included in the assessable value of the goods manufactured by the appellants. The Department issued show cause notices under section 4 (4)( d)( i) of the Act alleging that the appellants had collected the " wholesale price " of the Ro lled W o ven's supplied by the buyer and not the " cost of packing " incurred by the appellant's customer in buying the Ro ller and therefore, they were liable to pay excise duty on the " value " in respect of the " retail sale price " recovered by the manufacturer from the buyer. The Assistant Collector confirmed the demands raised by the Assistant Collector but allowed the appeals filed by the respondents. In appeal before the Collector of Central Excise, the Appellate Tribunal held that the " price " in relation to the " delivery " of " Pr est " in the wholesale trade is only the " amount " actually paid or payable by the seller to the buyer for the purpose of filling up the " component parts " of Ro lled Pr inted W o van " which is packed in " Pr open y " condition ". The Revenue contended that since the " pr iced Ro lled " Ro inted Ro ller / Pr inted System " is a separate product and is not capable of being sold as such, it cannot be said that the price of the Pr inted Pr inted Roll ing machine is not the price charged for the'Pr inted Fo il'brand. Dismis sing the Appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The concept of " wholesale cash " and the concept of'wholesale cash price'are distinct and have been introduced into the concept by the amendment of the definition of " transaction value " with effect from 16. 2. 1983. [ 10 B C ] 2. The expression " wholesale " has been defined in section 2 (d)( ii) of Section 4 of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944. It means " wholesale or retail " wholesale. The word " wholesale ", according to its dictionary meaning, means " one who sells wholesale or wholesale goods in wholesale ". The word'wholesale'is generally used in the sense of a person carrying on business; it is also used in contrad ist in ction to the words'wholesale '. The word is normally understood in popular parlance as including within its ambit the element of wholesale trading. Therefore, the word'wholes er'must mean a person who sells his own goods in retail. The term'wholesale trade'is ordinarily understood to mean " wholesale trade " or " wholesale trading " etc. and not " wholesale dealing " in any particular case. [ 11 E F G ] 3. The words " wholesale'and " wholesale wholesale trade "' have been construed by this Court in Union of India vs God f rey Ph illi Decision and Holding: A. I. R. 1984 S. C. 12 31, referred to.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5 (2) read with section 5. I. P. C. and section 161, I. PC. He was tried by a Magistrate on charge under section 161 I. Ps. for accepting bribe from PW 1 who had received Rs. 100 in cash as illegal gratification. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 471 I. p. c. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption created by section 4 (1) is rebut table and not merely conclusive. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) Section 5 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is not attracted because the presumption arises only when there is proof that the accused person has received any gratification other than legal remuneration. [ 463 E ] (ii) The presumption arising under section 4 is rebutted by proof. It is established that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the sup position that it exists. If the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption will arise. But if the explanation does not support the presumption, the statutory presumption will not come into play. [ 464 B D ] (iii) The evidence adduced by the prosecution regarding the receipt of money by the appellant from PW 3, the Principal's office, shows that he received the amount of Rs. 125 in the canteen when his wife refused to pay the same. The explanation given by the witness is plausible. The presumption created is not rebutted. [ 465 G H; 466 A ] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the demand made by PW 1 was true. The High court was right.

The petitioner was a tenant of the respondent company. He filed an application under section 630 (1) Cr. P. C. for recovery of possession of certain property from the respondent, who was the Managing Director of the Company and also against the employees of the company. The Magistrate dismissed the application on the ground that the petitioner had not been served with any notice or summons as required by section 630 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal to the Sessions Judge, the High Court held that the provisions of section 630 were not applicable to the present case because there was no evidence whatsoever to show that the respondent was in occupation of the premises at the time when he was employed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) Section 630 (l)( b) is independent of section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code and therefore, the words " any such property of the person employed " occurring in section 630 would include the present officers and employees; (ii) since the expression'any such officer or employee'used in section 629 (l) includes past officers and staff, the word'or'should be read as'and '. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: (1)( a) The expression'or ', appearing before the words'any other officer or servant of a company'in section 631 must be construed as having reference to the existing officers and servants of the same company. [ 591 G ] (b) The use of the expression " any other service " in section 6 (1), does not mean that the definition of the term'officer'in clause (a) of section 2 of the Act has to be confined only to those officers and employ ments which are mentioned therein but do not include any past officer or employees. [ 592 E F ] (c) The words'other officer'and'employee'have both the meanings given to them in section 5 (1). They cannot be read dis jun ctive ly so as to make the provision inapplicable to the former. [ 594 B ] (d) The contention that the expression,'any officer or other employee'means the officer or the employee of the firm whose name is entered in the register of companies, is not correct. The expression " officer or person " in sub section (1); (e) is wide enough to cover every officer or official of the Government who is authorised to execute the work of the office or of the establishment. It is true that the words used in subsection (1 A) are " any officer " and " employee ". But these words are qualified by the context in which they occur. The words " other than the officer " in the context mean subordinate officer or any other person who may be named in the order. [ 595 H ] (2) The word " officer " is defined in section 2 (h) of the Companies Act, 1956, to mean any person who is appointed by the Central Government or by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions of the Registrar under the Act.

The appellant was the sole trustee of a public temple. He had been managing the affairs of the said temple for several years and he was also one of the trustees in the said festival. In 1947, the appellant's father made an application to the Charity Commissioner under section 72 (1) of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950 for permission to hold the temple as private trust. The Assistant Charity Commissioner granted permission to him to open the temple on certain terms and conditions. On January 5, 1952, the Assistant Charity commissioner issued notice to the appellant stating that the temple was not a private temple but it was a private trust and therefore the provisions of sections 2 (13) and 32 were not applicable to it. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Assistant Commissioner dated August 31, 1957. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief because the deity was not the owner of the property. Allow ing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The primary question which arises for determination is whether the temple is a private or public temple within the meaning of section 2 (14) of The Bombay Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments Act, 1948. [ 531 A B ] 2. The definition of " private " in section 2 of the Act includes all persons who are connected with the management of a religious institution and are either servants of the State or of a local authority. The word " person " has not been defined in the Act. It is clear from the definition of the expression " person interested " in the explanation to section 2 that every person who is interested in the administration of a trust must be a person who either directly or indirectly employ es some personal or private interest. The expression " interested in such offer ings " in sec. 2 (15) means " interested " or " interested by whom soever ". The definition does not cover only cases where there is no direct relationship between the person whose interest is affected by the act of the trustee or his legal representative. The words " interested ", " interested himself " and " interested person " do not necessarily mean that the person who claims the right should have some direct interest in the matter. The present case falls under section 73 (1)( b) of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1951. [ 532 D E F ] 3. The object of the provision is to prevent the interference of the worship pers of the temple in the manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those who are interested in it. [ 533 C D ] 4. The fact that the devo tee may have a direct interest of his own in the property would not make him a person interested in a public trust within the definition given in section 3 (13).

The Punjab Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, was passed by the State Legislature in June 1949. Section 3 of the Act provided that all agricultural income tax shall be payable by a co operative society for every year on or before the 1st day of July following the year in which it is due and such income shall be deemed to have been assessed as if it were income received from business. The assessee's case was that he had not paid any amount by way of sales tax during the assessment years 1955 58 and 1956 51 and therefore no notice under section 13 could be issued. The Income tax Officer rejected this contention and held that there was nothing wrong with the order of assessment made by him. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. In further appeal to the Tribunal the High Court held that the proviso to section 46 (2) did not apply because the proceedings were initiated after the date of the amendment and since the proviso applied only to cases where the assessment was made prior to the amendment, the proviso would not apply. Held: (1) The words " any person " in section 46 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, mean a person who pays any sum to an assessee otherwise than as representing the income from whatever source derived. The word " person " has not been defined in the Act but its ordinary meaning is given to it in the sense of a jur istic person or jur istic persons. The definition of " person ", however wide, cannot be confined to legal entities like a company or other body corporate. It must include a jur id ical entity. A quasi corporation may be a legal entity or a separate legal entity. But the legislature can make a law imposing liability upon a non resident for income tax purposes even though the statute does not expressly provide for such a liability. The fact that the legislature has chosen to impose a liability on a non - resident to pay taxes on behalf of his principal does not mean that the fiction created by the legislature is intended to be limited to those cases where a person is sought to be taxed by the enactment of a different Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1944. It had a factory at village B ich hat re, and it carried on its business from the beginning till about the middle of the year 1943. In the course of this business the appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the sale of its products to the latter. On December 15, 1953, the appellant issued a notice under section 9A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, calling upon the respondent to show cause why the workmen should not be dismissed for breach es of the provisions of the. The respondent replied that the workmen were not entitled to any wages as they were paid only Rs. 3 per day. The appellant's case was that the respondent had no right to demand or pay bonus for over 12 hours every week but the workmen did not agree to it. The Tribunal held that the strike was illegal because the workmen could not be said to have been given work for more than 9 hours in a day. Held, that the contention of the appellant that the period of rest was less than 48 hours is correct. The fact that the weekly off days were fixed by the employers would not make any difference if the weekly holidays were less than 8 hours. The workmen were entitled to payment of overtime wages for over time and if there was any delay in paying them beyond 48 hours, the workmen would be entitled to wages for the over time.

The appellant tenant was in occupation of a building which was constructed on the land belonging to him. He filed an application for eviction of the tenant under Section 20 (1)( b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 before the Rent Controller who allowed the same and directed that he would not be evicted from the premises. On appeal by the respondent landlord the Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Rent Control Officer and restored the decree passed by the trial court. In revision the High Court held that since the provisions of this Act were applicable only to ten years and therefore so far as the period prior to the commencement of the tenancy is concerned it will not apply and accordingly dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provision contained in sub section (2) of Section 2 of the Act is clear that during the pendency of the litigation even of 10 years and thereafter no suit for eviction can be instituted except on specified grounds. [ 167 D ] 2. 1 The expression " at any time " used in Section 20 means " at the end of the proceeding ". It does not mean that the proceedings are pending for a long time but it must be determined after hearing the parties or their representatives. [ 168 C ] 2: 3. The words'at the beginning of the proceedings'occurring in Section 2 (e) of this act should be construed as including the stage when the suit is finally disposed of. [ 169 F G ] 3. 2 The word'at'has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary, 5th Edition, Vol. I, page 12 71; Web ster's New International Dictionary, Volume II, page 15 99; Web sters Third New International dictionary, referred to.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent landlord. On April 26, 1949 he filed an application under section 3 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1949 for ejectment on the ground that his tenancy had been determined by the Controller in accordance with law and as such there was no question of his being evicted from the premises. The Rent Controller held that the appellant's claim to be a th ika tenant could not be sustained because the provisions of the Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy Act were applicable to him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions contained in sections 4 and 5 of the Act did not apply to the facts of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (1) that section 4 of the, which provided that " every tenant shall be deemed to have purchased from his landlord the land held by him as a th ikar or si rd ar, as the case may be, under section 6; (2) that the proviso to section 3 (1)( b) of the said Act applied only to suits and appeals pending on the date of commencement of the Ordinance and not to decrees passed before the enactment of the amending Act of 1953; (3) that since the amendment of 1953 the definition of a th ik tenancy given in section 3 was prospective, the bar created by section 4 would not apply and the decree passed after the coming into force of the Amending Act of 1952 was not exec utable. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) Section 4 of Act No. 51 of 1948 is retrospective in operation and therefore the provision of section 4 will have to be read down so as to give effect to the provisions thereof. [ 184 G ] (ii) The language of section 3 is clear and unambiguous and does not require any interpretation. It has to be construed strictly. [ 185 C D ] (iii) The words " notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force " mean all things done or omitted to be done under the Act before the passing of the order but do not include any proceeding under the relevant statute. If the legislature intended to exclude the operation of section 5 of Act 53 of 1953, then the word " shall " used in section 4 must be given its ordinary meaning.

The appellant was appointed as a Bench Secretary Grade I in the Central Government. He was promoted to the post of Bench Secretaries Grade II on January 29, 1986. On his promotion to the said post he was placed at par with other Bench Secretaries who were selected by the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 3 (1) of the Indian Administrative Service (Fixation of Pay and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1954. In the year 1987, the State Government issued an order fixing the pay scale of Bench Secretary Gr. I as Rs. 150 - 300. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the fixation of his pay scale. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant had been given higher pay scale than the one which he was drawing earlier. The Division Bench directed payment of higher pay scales to him. The appeal preferred by the Union of India against the judgment of the High court was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for equal work is not only a matter of policy but also a guide factor. [ 305 F ] 2. The concept of equal treatment has no rational ity or relevance to be put in cold storage. It is based on human reason and is founded on justice and equality. It must be something whose colour is p iv otal. It bears similarity to each other. There is inherent danger in treating unequal's as equals. A classification should not be artificial or arbitrary. It has a rational nexus with the object of the Act. It should be based on some qualities or characteristics of persons group ed together and not in others who are left out. The impugned order of the Tribunal directing the appellants to pay the revised pay scale to the respondent cannot be sustained. [ 306 E G ] 3. The decision of this Court in All India Radio and Others vs Union of india, [ 1985 ] Supp. SCC 191, does not lay down any proposition that differential treatment between two groups of Judges is discriminatory. [ 307 B ] 4. The classification made under the Rules is reasonable and valid. [ 308 C ] 5. The fact that the petitioner was appointed in the same capacity as the respondent No. 3 would not make any difference since it is not shown that there was any discrimination. [ 309 D ] 6. The contention that the High Courts have committed error in considering all the three cadres differently from the single cadre does not hold water. [ 310 H; 311 A ] 7. 1. In view of the above discussion, the High Powered Committee was justified in recommending the case of the appellant for placement in the next higher grade.

The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Under section 2 (d) of the U. P. Municipalities Act, 19 16, a municipality constituted under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, was empowered to impose tax on lands and buildings within its limits. Section 69 (d), which provided for the compulsory imposition of property tax, provides that every Municipality shall levy a tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Section 133 of the said Act provided that the power conferred by the Act upon the State Government to impose any tax or rate imposed by a municipality under the Act would be exercised by it subject to such restrictions and modifications as may be specified therein. Section 132 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Tax Act, 1949, provided that no person shall impose any building or land or erect any building in contravention of the provisions thereof, unless he had given notice in writing to the Commissioner of his intention so to do. Section 134 provided that where any building is erected or re - erected without sanction or permission in contravention thereof, the Chief Officer of the Municipality shall forthwith cause the same to be removed from the premises and levied a tax thereon at such rate not exceeding six per cent um, as the State Legislature may specify in this behalf. Section 135 A provided for appeal against the order of assessment made under section 133 of a municipality. Section 136 provided that an appeal shall lie to the State government against any decision or order passed by the municipal authorities under the Central Act. The respondent 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid provision contending that the resolution of the Board dated January 28, 1976, was invalid because: (i) there was no valid sanction accorded by the State; (ii) the notification issued by the President did not have the force of law; and (iii) the municipality was not competent to impose the tax in question. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the municipality had no jurisdiction to impose a tax on land and buildings under section 127 A of the Municipalities Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression " municipal area " has been defined in section 2 of the Municipal Corporations Act, 18 88, but does not include a cant onment. [ 128 C ] (2) The word'municipality'occurring in section 129 of the Madhya Municipalities Act means a municipal corporation. It includes a municipal committee. Therefore, the municipality constituted for the purpose of levying the tax must be deemed to be a municipality within the meaning of section 2 sub section (b) of that Act. [ 131 G ] (3) The municipality is a municipality and therefore, the Act applies to the municipality. There is nothing in the Act to prevent the municipality from imposing the tax on the lands and building belonging to the Municipality. The municipality was a municipality which was created under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act and the municipality came into existence only after the enactment of the municipality Act. If the municipality were to be regarded as a municipality, then the municipality could impose the property tax under section 130 of the Maharashtra Municipal Act, 1961.

The appellant, a private limited company, was granted a lease by the Government of Madras under r. 47 (1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 for a period exceeding one year. Under cl. (b) of sub rule (3), the lessee is required to pay annually at the rate of Rs. 30 per ton ne of ordinary sand extracted from the leased area and royalty at the rates specified in the second proviso to r. 49. Clause (c) provides that the lessee shall not be entitled to any compensation or damages on account of such fixation. In exercise of the powers conferred by r. 4 (2)( d) of Regulation XX IV of the Coal Mines Regulations, 1948, the Central Government issued a notification dated July 1, 1945, fixing the lease rent payable by the appellant for a sum of Rs, 10, 000 / per year. The appellant's writ petition challenging the validity of this notification was dismissed by the High Court. On appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) that the appellant had no right to terminate the leasehold rights created after July 1. 1945; (ii) that there was no provision in the Act which authorised the Government to determine the lease; and (iii) that even if the lease was determined under the third proviso, the appellant could have no legal right to continue the lease beyond the said term. HELD: (1)( a) The first proviso to section 20 (2) of'the Act is only an enabling provision and does not affect the validity Of the second Proviso. It is true that the second condition laid down in the third clause is satisfied if the lessee has been given an option to purchase the land within the period prescribed therein but that option is subject to certain conditions. The third proviso to that sub section says that " where the lessor accepts the grant without any further necessity for any similar concession, he may, at his discretion, accept such terms as he thinks fit ". This clearly shows that the third condition is also made subject to some other provisions of the Act. [ 562 C D ] (2). The third condition applies to leases granted before July 1 1945, when the appellant applied for renewal of the lease. If the third Proviso comes into operation, the question arises whether the termination of the leasehold right created after January 27, 1952, can be challenged. There is nothing in the fourth proviso to show that the Government must take notice of the application of the third exception. [ 563 G H ] (3) The third Proviso to section 13 (2), however, makes it clear that the lease will be terminated only upon the three months'notice being served on the party concerned. The last proviso to the third paragraph lays down that the termination should be effected before the expiry of the original lease. The word'may'in the first proviso means that the authority to decide whether the lease should be terminated or allowed to subsist will mean the Government should do something to avoid the same.
